Hi Ben, Thanks a lot for taking your time to work with my model.  I appreciate it.  My model was a very planned expedition into stan.   I've been reading documentation and asking questions on the list, along-the-way, to both understand whether stan was possible and to focus the effort.  You guys have been very generous in providing tip and tricks.

Relative to the parameter matrix, Lambda_s, it represents loadings of a factor analytic construction from one of my covariance matrices.   To rotationally identify this model, I must restrict the structure of Lambda_s in some way; that is, to set certain entries to a fixed value.  You may know that a typical approach (Muirhead) restricts the loadings matrix to lower triangular.   I accomplish this restriction by term-by-term multiplying (hadamard or schur product) the D x K, Lambda_s by a D x K "pick" matrix, B, filled with 0's and 1's to enforce the lower triangular restriction.   I then place an informative N(0,1) prior on the elements of Lambda_s.  The idea is that the likelihood doesn't inform the upper triangular elements of Lambda_s, but the proper prior would anyway produce a proper posterior so all should be well.  I ran this idea by Bob and he thought it should work fine.   Of course, this construction probably doesn't explain why the elements of Lambda_s go to nan.  I will have to think about that.

Hi Toby, I've not yet been able to get my model to run, though it does compile relatively quickly (even under optimization level -O3).  In my view, my model is not nearly so complicated as it looks.   The unique twist is that parameter objects in this model are multivariate under unknown covariance structures.   Ben explained that using the multivariate Gaussian is parameterized in the covariance matrix.  So the automated differentiator that compose the gradient of the log joint probability will have to invert this matrix on every sampling step.   Further, one of the covariance matrices in my model is composed from a factor analytic structure.  So if my loadings matrix is D x K where K < D, I can use the Woodbury Sherman matrix identity and accomplish a D x D inversion of a covariance matrix through a smaller K x K inversion (with some associated matrix products).   All to say, it should be faster to perform the inversions, once, and then directly update lp__.

If I get the model to work, I will write back about runtimes.  That said, I'm confused on how the speed will compare to JAGS for similar models.   JAGS is relatively slow and I don't expect stan to be any faster - even after accounting for the greater informativeness of each stan iteration.   The graphical model nodal parameterization of JAGS, however, is a function of the number of observations in my data, so as that goes up, the runtimes go up (with an amount depending, in part, on the relationship between number of observations and number of model parameters).   I was hoping that stan would prove much more scalable in the number of data observations.  If so, I wouldn't have to code my own models for larger datasets.  After all, 2 days per run is worth it if it save me development time (unless i'm running monte carlo simulations).

terrance.

On 10/1/12 1:16 PM, terrance savitsky wrote:
>..

>
> If I get the model to work, I will write back about runtimes.  That said, I'm confused on how the speed will compare to
> JAGS for similar models.   JAGS is relatively slow and I don't expect stan to be any faster - even after accounting for
> the greater informativeness of each stan iteration.

When JAGS can use conjugate priors, it applies
proper Gibbs sampling, with independent draws from
the condtional.  In those cases, JAGS will be scale
invariant.

NUTS without varying stepsize adaptation is rotation
invariant.  NUTS with varying stepsize adaptation (the
default sampler in Stan) is not technically either, but
has a bit of the advantages of both.

If you have a problem that does not have a lot of
correlation among the posterior parameters AND is
conjugate, JAGS will almost certainly be faster than
Stan and continue to be so in the future.

In both JAGS and Stan, it can often help to reparameterize
to remove some of the direct dependence.  There's a discussion
of this process for JAGS in both of Andrew's books,
the regression book with Jennifer and Bayesian Data Analysis.
The next edition of BDA will discuss doing this with Stan,
as will our next manual.

We've had a lot of sucess so far in pulling out the means,
as I do in the item-response models in the current user's guide.
I'm writing a new chapter for the user's guide on variable
transforms and reparameterizations that will go into more
detail.

Ben's been outlining code transforms that can help for
multivariates.  We also plan to introduce some new data
structures (triangular, symmetric, and cholesky factor
matrices) and vectorize some more operations there to make
Stan faster (we probably have at least a factor of 5--50 or so
combining better partial-eval auto-dif and vectorization).

 > ... I was hoping that stan would

 > prove much more scalable in the number of data observations.  If so, I wouldn't have to code my own models for larger
 > datasets.  After all, 2 days per run is worth it if it save me development time (unless i'm running monte carlo
 > simulations).

I haven't done controlled comparisons, but Stan should
scale much better in terms of how much memory it takes
per variable.  That will depend heavily for Stan on
what kinds of probability distributions are used.  If
they need iterative linear algebra algorithms, Stan
can wind up taking up a lot of memory, too.

The reimplementations with vectorization will help with
scaling as will partial evals in auto-dif (fewer intermediate
expression template classes to store).

- Bob

Sorry -- didn't realize the ball was in my court.

I'd guess that test_grad is not technically hanging
(for instance, check your activity monitor or equivalent
on your system), but rather grinding away calculating
finite differences.  We've found it to be rather slow
for large numbers of parameters with complex ops.

It should get a factor of four or five faster as soon as
I get around to templating out the log_prob function
in the generated models -- then we can use the version without
calculating the gradients as well.

My global suggestion is to try simpler models first and
gradually add structure.  For instance, try a diagonal
covariance matrix first and see if you can get that working.
Or fix the variance component at something reasonable and
fit the rest of the model.  The specifics, of course, depend
on the model.

- Bob

work and build up to the more complex model?  It's

>     divide two infinite values.
>
>
> I don't think there are any logs or divisions involved here.

There are logs implicit everywhere in Stan because we use log
probabilities.  There are probably divisions in the solvers
used over the covariance matrices you produce that are based
on Lambda_s.

 > I am guessing that the gradient goes NaN somehow and that
> propagates. That guess is based on the fact that --test_grad hangs.

That won't cause --test_grad to hang.  It'll
report NaN.  That's why we wrote it.

As I said before, I'm guessing test_grad is just
slow, not hanging.

It can take as much time to run test_grad as to run
10s, 100s or even 1000s of iterations of Stan depending
on the posterior geometry and the number of params.

- Bob

The directory into which something unpacks is
usually the "home" directory.

> and making libstan.a and stanc.

These should be in the home/bin

> I interpret a "home directory" as some type of
> installation would take place that produces a directory named "stan".  that's apparently not how the process works.

This is done differently by different systems.
Some pull out just the name (as R does), some pull
out name/version and some just name-version.

We decided to go the name-version route.

This is a common strategy that's employed by
both Boost and Eigen (as well as all of the Java
Apache projects and Java itself).

> While not in the directions for Windows, I assume I need to perform an update to the PATH environment variable in order
> to compile a .stan file (when not in stan-src-1.0.2).

I'd suggest building from <stan-home> using the makefile.
Our makefile doesn't work from other paths (though we
hope to fix that in the future).

If you want to build without the makefile, then
yes, you need to put <stan-home>/bin/stanc on the PATH
to translate a .stan file to C++ using stanc.
And you also need to change the library paths or
create environment variables for those relative
to STAN_HOME.

A common approach is to define a variable
STAN_HOME that points to the directory containing
the makefile into which Stan unpacks.

Then add %STAN_HOME%\bin to the path in Windows.

You can also define an EIGEN_LIB variable as
%STAN_HOME%/lib/...,  etc.

> It also bears noting that the new "print" command doesn't print to the R layer for those compiling and running from there.

This should work in Stan 1.0.2.  Jiqiang just
plumbed in the R stdout and stderr.

How are you running R?

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I have taken Bob's advice and successively whittled down the model to center around the elements that are causing the sampling errors.  I attach a much-reduced model - with nearly all of the computational efficiencies removed for quick readability.   Associated data are also attached.  This reduced model produces the same errors as we've previously encountered; in particular, the sampler is not able to find a sufficiently small step size.  i have occasionally also received the error message that a matrix is not symmetric.  I would sincerely appreciate your having one more look ...

The model employs 2 sets of multivariate ordinal responses, y1[N1,D] and y2[N2,D] for each of two measurement modes.   These data are modeled in an ordinal logistic model with ordered cutpoints, gamma1[D,ncut], gamma2[D,ncut] and a common set of intrinsic traits, matrix[D,2] Delta[T].   Each column represents a mode.   The Delta[T] are modeled as zero mean matrix variate normal with density kernel (up to a proportionality constant), |S_m|^{-D} |S_d|^{-M} exp(-0.5 trace[ S_d^{-1} Delta[t] S_m^{-1} Delta[t]').   Covariance matrices S_d are D x D and S_m are (M=2) x (M=2). Finally, S_d = Lambda * Lambda' + diag(the_del), is composed under a factor analytic structure.

Here's what I think is happening:   the sampler is unable to retain numerical stability for a covariance matrix constructed in a factor analytic manner and the resulting computed covariance matrix, S_d, is violating symmetric, positive definiteness.   I already have informative N(0,1) priors on Lambda.  I tried an alternative to restrict the signs to positive, but no effect.  The 2 x 2 S_m covariance matrix receives an lkj prior.  I tried replacing that with an inv_wishart with no change in results.

If the problem is what I think it is, we're seeing a curse of dimensionality problem expressing itself in numerical instability.   Conjugacy restricts posterior objects to readily computed algebraic forms which helps stability.  Similarly, sequential scan sampling - block-by-block - probably also produces a more numerically stable sampler than jointly sampling the entire parameter space in each metropolis step.

Thanks for your help,

Terrance.

our open-access lists over proprietary communications.
One reason is that we're already drowning in complex user
models and if we take them on one-by-one off the list,
we have to deal with them one-by-one rather than hopefully
building up some group expertise so users can help each
other in the future.

If you use cygwin, you should use Unix-style paths, not

This is an issue we need to fix, but it's
not fatal.   Actually, it won't come up in
1.0.2 because we trap and throw errors if users
try to define discrete parameters.

>

This is the killer.  You use a variable named 'nil' without
defining it.

My guess without seeing your model is that you used an int
parameter -- that gets flagged in 1.0.2 with an error message.

Stan doesn't support int params.

On 10/1/12 5:51 PM, terrance savitsky wrote:
> I have taken Bob's advice and successively whittled down the model to center around the elements that are causing the
> sampling errors.  I attach a much-reduced model - with nearly all of the computational efficiencies removed for quick
> readability.   Associated data are also attached.  This reduced model produces the same errors as we've previously
> encountered; in particular, the sampler is not able to find a sufficiently small step size.  i have occasionally also
> received the error message that a matrix is not symmetric.  I would sincerely appreciate your having one more look ...
>
> The model employs 2 sets of multivariate ordinal responses, y1[N1,D] and y2[N2,D] for each of two measurement modes.
> These data are modeled in an ordinal logistic model with ordered cutpoints, gamma1[D,ncut], gamma2[D,ncut] and a common
> set of intrinsic traits, matrix[D,2] Delta[T].   Each column represents a mode.   The Delta[T] are modeled as zero mean
> matrix variate normal with density kernel (up to a proportionality constant), |S_m|^{-D} |S_d|^{-M} exp(-0.5 trace[
> S_d^{-1} Delta[t] S_m^{-1} Delta[t]').   Covariance matrices S_d are D x D and S_m are (M=2) x (M=2). Finally, S_d =
> Lambda * Lambda' + diag(the_del), is composed under a factor analytic structure.
>
> Here's what I think is happening:   the sampler is unable to retain numerical stability for a covariance matrix
> constructed in a factor analytic manner and the resulting computed covariance matrix, S_d, is violating symmetric,
> positive definiteness.

Symmetry should be under your direct control if
you construct the covariance matrix.

One option is to copy one side into the other:

   for (m in 1:rows(S_d))
     for (n in (m+1):cols(S_d))
        S_d[m,n] = S_d[n,m];

though I don't see how defining

   S_d =  Lambda * Lambda' + diag(the_del)

is going to break symmetry.

> I already have informative N(0,1) priors on Lambda.  I tried an alternative to restrict the
> signs to positive, but no effect.

I don't know what you mean by "restrict".  Just
adding truncation won't do it -- you need to declare
the variables as constrained.  Also, by "no effect"
do you mean "didn't solve the problem" or "didn't
restrict to positive"?

> The 2 x 2 S_m covariance matrix receives an lkj prior.  I tried replacing that with
> an inv_wishart with no change in results.
>
> If the problem is what I think it is, we're seeing a curse of dimensionality problem expressing itself in numerical
> instability.   Conjugacy restricts posterior objects to readily computed algebraic forms which helps stability.
>   Similarly, sequential scan sampling - block-by-block - probably also produces a more numerically stable sampler than
> jointly sampling the entire parameter space in each metropolis step.

My own speculation on why things break is almost always wrong.

We haven't run into any critical numerical issues we haven't
been able to solve yet, but then we haven't really hammered
on covariance matrices either.

I should change the test_grad to print out incrementally.
As is, it computes all the gradients then returns the answer.
At least this would let people know it's slow, not hung,
as well as providing some useful feedback.

- Bob

I think the problem is with this step:   S_d =  Lambda * Lambda' + diag(the_del).    My sense from stripping away everything is that the Lambda*Lambda' construction becomes numerically imprecise under joint sampling such that asymmetry is introduced under a relatively low magnitude diag(the_del).

On Monday, October 1, 2012 6:37:25 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Symmetry should be under your direct control if
> you construct the covariance matrix.
>
> One option is to copy one side into the other:
>
>    for (m in 1:rows(S_d))
>      for (n in (m+1):cols(S_d))
>         S_d[m,n] = S_d[n,m];
>
> though I don't see how defining
>
>    S_d =  Lambda * Lambda' + diag(the_del)
>
> is going to break symmetry.

It can happen numerically, but it probably means the check for symmetry doesn't have enough tolerance. Since Lambda is triangular, you could use the multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(Lambda) function or (in git's master branch) tcrossprod(Lambda). Either of those should preserve symmetry.

Ben

n 10/2/12 1:44 AM, Freddy López wrote:

> I'm trying to fit a model considering a distribution that is not part from stan. In the past, I have used zeros or ones
> trick like those describe here:
>
> http://users.aims.ac.za/~mackay/BUGS/Manuals/Tricks.html#SpecifyingANewSamplingDistribution
>
> I have read we can define new distributions (pag. 55, stan-reference-1.0.2.pdf) but I need define a distribution with
> two or three parameters.
>
> So, I don't know what is the best option. There exist some zeros or ones trick strategies using stan can you show me?
> Should I define a new distribution like that indicated in pag. 55? In that case, have you got an example with using
> parameters?

No, you don't need the 0/1 trick.    Just add the log
probability to lp__ as in the example in the user's
guide.  (I'll add the next example, too.)

Here's an example involving the direct coding of the
exponential distribution with inverse scale lambda:

   lp__ <- lp__ + log(lambda) - lambda * y;

If lambda is a variable, this produces C++ code very
much like that produced by:

   y ~ exponential(lambda);

If lambda is a constant, the above sampling expression
is smart enough to drop the log(lambda) term -- you only
need the log probability up to an additive constant.

Also, the sampling statement checks domain bounds so
that lambda is positive and y non-negative.

I just added that example to the manual.

If you're entering an obfuscated Stan model contest,
you can also use the 0/1 trick.  The exponential would
look like:

   0 ~ poisson(C - (log(lambda) - lambda * y));

where C is a data-dependent magic number big enough to
ensure the argument to the poisson is positive (Stan doesn't
care about additive constants and is also smart enough to
drop the normalizing term because of the fixed outcome
count 0).

- Bob

On 10/2/12 7:56 AM, Andrew Tanentzap wrote:
> Hi Bob

Just as a matter of form, this is an open list, so
posts shouldn't really be addressed to me personally!

> So just to clarify, even if I know the rate of my Poisson distribution, and simply want to sample from it randomly, I
> can't do this at present because it requires specifying the expectations as "integers" and "parameters"?...  And I can't
> sample in any of the other "non-parameter" blocks...

Let me first try to clarify terminology:

   poisson(y|lambda) = ...

   y: non-negative integer outcome (aka the variate)
   lambda: non-negative real value

For the Poisson, the value of parameter lambda just
happens to be the mean of the distribution (and
variance in this case).  And also the expectation of
any random variable distributed as Poisson(lambda).

Following BUGS, we call any unknown variable a parameter.
And y is restricted to integers.   But y is not an
expectation, so I wonder if we're talking
about the same thing.

Stan is fine sampling lambda as a parameter.

Stan cannot (yet) sample an unknown integer y.  Not
in any of the blocks.   We're going to add sampling
in the derivated quantities block, but that will only
work to draw random integers from a distribution
like Poisson(lambda).  You won't be able to use them
as latent responsibility indicators in mixture models,
for instance, because there's no way to transfer information
from the derived quantities block back to the model.

- Bob

On 10/2/12 7:49 AM, Andrew Tanentzap wrote:
> Really??  I thought the expected value of a Poisson has to be discrete
> (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_distribution)...
>
> The STAN reference manual (v1.0.1) also says on pg 122 that the expectation "n" has to be an integer.

What's going on with Poisson?  Did we botch something in
the manual?  It looks OK to me.  It's just that n is
not an expectation in any sense of the word I understand.

Let me try to clarify.  Here's the density function:

   Poisson(y|lambda) = (exp(-lambda) / lambda!) * lambda^y

   y:  the variate, an integer >= 0

   lambda: the location parameter, a real > 0

If Y is an integer random variable and Y has
a Poisson(lambda) distribution, i.e., Y ~ Poisson(lambda),
then the expectation of Y is lambda.

Sometimes people conflate means (properties of
densities), expectations (properties of random variables),
and location parameters (parameters of distributions).

> It threw up an
> error that suggested this when I tried switching my missing parameter to a "real".

As it should.  y has to be an integer as declared in
the manual.

What people were suggesting is that you could write
your own probability density and fudge the result
by treating y as real in that density.  See the
citation in an earlier e-mail, for example.  I don't
know enough about this strategy to tell you if or
how well it'd work.

> Perhaps, I'm misunderstanding the point you're trying to make?

If the above didn't help, maybe you should take some time
to read up on expectations in general and the Poisson
distribution in particular.

- Bbo

I've tracked the issue down.  There are two issues at play.

One is there appears to be a bug with the step size selection code.
I'm not sure what's going on exactly, but turning it off (setting a
fixed step size with epsilon=0.0001 for instance) allows sampling to
proceed.  (I'm not sure if this is exposed through the R interface or
not.)  Matt, do you have time to check whats happening with the
stepsize adaption in this case?  The fixed epsilon works just fine.

The other issue is that inverse is not certain to return a symmetric
matrix when called on a symmetric matrix.  As a result Sd_inv (and
maybe Sm_inv) would become asymmetric after a point due to numerical
issues.  This is numerical precision issue which could be worked
around explicitly if you wanted, but the easy fix is to remove the
declarations of Sd_inv and Sm_inv from the transformed parameters
block and put them in the model block as local variables.  There may
also be an issue with symmetry testing not selecting thresholds
appropriately but the fact that this is being hit likely reflects that
the covariance matrices S_d (and/or S_m) are becoming singular.

Hope this helps.

As an aside, Bob, how hard would be it to catch transformation
exceptions when they're thrown in the model code and report the
variable name they arose on?  Alternatively could we propogate the
model level expressions and/or variable names down through the calls
in case exceptions are thrown?  The hardest part of debugging this was
figuring out exactly which matrix was failing the symmetry test which
required the use of gdb.

Cheers,
Marcus

by hand.

Anything you can do to avoid actually doing an inverse
might help.  We have the MATLAB-style left and right
residual operators, which you can often use instead, or

> All said, what do you think causes the numerical imprecision in the inverse
> computations?   The two covariance matrices in my model are relatively low
> dimension -  one is 10 x 10 and the other, 2 x 2.   Is there some drift
> introduced in the repeated gradient computations in the automated
> differentiator?  I've built gaussian process models, before, where it is
> standard to add a diagonal "nugget" to stabilize inversion under high
> dimensions, but that doesn't seem the case here.   (I had also used a
> simpler version of HMC based on analytic differentiation).

It shouldn't really have anything to do with the size of the matrix.
Rather, if I had to guess, the values of s_m or s_d were getting very
small.  If they become zero, the resulting covariance matrices are
singular but nearby the inverse matrix will be unstable.  Since
inverse() doesn't know that the matrix is symmetric, it's not able to
ensure that the resulting matrix is also symmetric.  As Bob noted, you
could compute the inverse using the cholesky decomposition which is
numerically more stable. Even better though is to avoid computing the
inverse unless you absolutely must   Again as Bob mentioned, there are
functions which avoid the inverse and are much more numerically
stable.  mdivide_left(A,b) and mdivide_right(b,A) will give you A^-1
*b and b*A^-1 respectively.  See also mdivide_left_tri if you're using
the cholesky factors.  I'm not sure if they're exposed to the
modelling language yet.  Let me know if you need them and they're not
and I can maybe get that cleaned up.

> It would be super helpful to have variable names in error messages.  That
> said, the "print" statement will help, though that is not yet implemented to
> propagate print outputs to the R layer.

As noted, print should be there in the latest version.

Cheers,
Marcus

> It shouldn't really have anything to do with the size of the matrix.

my experience is that covariance matrices tend to become nearly singular in high dimensions due to numerical instability as it's hard to maintain SPD in high dimensions.   that's why a multivariate Gaussian with an unstructured covariance (not generated from lower dimensional constructs) becomes impractical under high dimensions.  Performing lower-dimensional projections and employing a nugget is common in the gaussian process literature.

> Rather, if I had to guess, the values of s_m or s_d were getting very
small.

Maybe this is the problem.  I did impose more informative priors on these objects, but with no improvement.

> mdivide_left(A,b) and mdivide_right(b,A) will give you A^-1

*b and b*A^-1 respectively.  Let me know if you need them and they're not

and I can maybe get that cleaned up.

I didn't find these functions in the stan manual.  I've used just such constructions (gaussian elimination with a cholesky decomposition to compute a quadratic product) - again in gaussian process models.  In my original stan script (before I extracted a simpler version), I avoided direct computation of a D x D inverse by using an idea from Ben to project to a lower-dimensional K x K matrix, where in my case, K = 3.   I had the same issue where the sampler couldn't find an acceptably small stepsize.

Big picture, your comment about singularity causing the stability problems may be quite correct.  Yet, the root cause of the singularity may not have anything to do with the inversion method and it's stability properties.  Unless there's something unusual going on behind the scenes in the automated differentiator, computing an inversion in each sampling iteration of a 3 x 3 SPD matrix wouldn't seem like it should be a problem.   When I take Marcus' tip on constraining the matrices to be symmetric, the symmetry errors - not surprisingly - go away.   They are replaced by the sampler being unable to find a sufficiently small stepsize.   It seems possible that there's some other sampling problem going on that creates singularity, which is the symptom, but not the cause of the problem.

The symmetry errors also go away (for me) when you just don't worry
about symmetry of the inverses.  Symmetry of the constructed
covariances is fine on my end.  You don't need to enforce it
explicitly.

There is definitely a sampler issue going on as it should be able to
find an appropriate stepsize but is giving up too early.  See my note
about using a fixed step size as an intermediate solution.  This
sampler problem will be harder to track down and may not have an
immediate fix.  You could play with the parameters of the nesterov
dual averaging a bit (--delta and --gamma are the relevant parameter

messages.body_plain:
> On Wed, Oct 3, 2012 at 10:22 AM, Lucas Leemann <llee...@gmail.com <mailto:llee...@gmail.com>> wrote:
>     I have a lot of binary explanatory variables. Does it matter whether I declare them as "int" or "real" with respect
>     to runtime?

On 10/3/12 10:24 AM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
 > int is, overall, the best option and should be a little bit faster.
 > That said, it won't be a big difference unless your
 > model is very small and very simple.

The last sentence is key -- you should do whatever's
natural for the data, which for binary variables, would
be int.

If they're parameters (unknown), they need to be real.

If they're not parameters, what's fastest will depend
on what you do with them.  One issue is that int is
32-bit and real is 64-bit, and smaller is usually faster.
So if you have an array of values and traverse them,
there's less memory paging for 32-bit values.
But if you have to take those ints which are not known
at compile time and convert them to doubles, that's
slower (but not nearly as slow as the reverse conversion
with floor(), round(), etc., or even a cast in C++), it
can be faster to just have them all be doubles.

- Bob

The key thing that I didn't realize until Matt explained

steps in the final half of the tree generated by NUTS.

accepted.  So the relation between target rejection and
duplicated samples (overall rejection in NUTS at an
iteration) will depend on the size of the tree (i.e., the
number of leapfrog steps).

Sorry for taking so long to weigh in, I've been ignoring my email lately.

The step size adaptation assumes that the accuracy of the Hamiltonian
simulation can always be increased to an acceptable range by
decreasing the step size. If this assumption is violated, then the
adaptation absolutely will not converge. Models with reasonably smooth
posteriors pretty much always satisfy this assumption. Numerical
problems (e.g. from trying to invert near-singular matrices) and
domain issues (e.g. from failing to constrain non-negative variables
or positive-definite matrices) can cause it to be violated.

My guess is that the adaptation failures will go away if the domain
issues (s_m and s_d being unconstrained) and the  numerical issues
(using matrix inversion instead of mdivide) people have brought up are
resolved.

Matt

messages.body_plain:
I had tried many of the steps you've suggested on my full model, but have now also tried your suggestions on the simplified model (that still produces the same errors as the  full model).   In short, the very same runtime errors persist.  Here's some of what I did:

1. I restricted the scale parameters (s_d, s_m) to be positive reals for composing the covariance matrices (S_d, S_m) from the correlation matrices (R_d, R_m), which receive lkj priors.

1.5.  I placed informative inv_gamma priors on scale parameters, s_d and s_m.

2. I replaced the above formulation with inverse wishart priors directly to the covariance matrices.   Part of my reasoning for trying such was that highly smoothing priors may do more (in a weak sense) to ensure smoothness of the posterior to help me get around the stepsize selection problem (even in a situation where conjugacy isn't used for sampling).  I recognize it shouldn't matter - so long as my model is identified - under a proper probability model, but i decided to anyway try.  Didn't help, as noted.

3. I, next, added back one piece of complexity by building the D x D (for D = 10) covariance matrix, S_d,  in a factor analytic / sparse construction with K = 3 factors.  Ben pointed out that the Woodbury Sherman matrix identity may be applied to recover the inverse of the D x D, S_d, by inverting a lower-dimensional K x K matrix.   Since the inverse of the  K x K matrix  is used in a quadratic formulation with a D x K (loadings) matrix, I first performed the cholesky decomposition of the K x K matrix, inverted it, and multiplied it by the transpose of the D x K loadings matrix and then took their quadratic product.   The other covariance matrix, S_m, is 2 x 2 and I just perform the direct inverse.

You've noted that the sampling goes off the rails pretty quickly.  It's counter-intuitive that inverting a 3 x 3 lower triangular and a 2 x 2 covariance matrix should cause such rapid failure.   Even if the inverse computation were numerically unstable that would likely accrue over iterations and it appears the sampler gets right away stuck.   Of course, I really have no idea.   Maybe there's something else incorrectly specified in my script that I'm not seeing.

 I've scripted a version of this model in JAGS with an unstructured (more general) D*M x D*M covariance matrix, rather than from the kronecker product of lower order D x D and M x M covariances.   The model is entirely conjugate (as I also employ a latent response for ordered outcomes), so JAGS handles it without issue.   I have a nagging doubt, however, about this data set because the signal is relatively weak so that the prior overly influences the posterior.   That's why I wanted to employ a more parsimonious structured covariance formulation in stan.   I don't think a lack of signal would ordinally cause stan to fail under smooth priors - e.g. a proper probability model; it should just return the prior, but maybe that's not the case.  I have other data under this project with a very strong signal in which I've performed similar modeling in JAGS.  when I have time, I will write a stan script for these data.  the model would be less complex, though still heavily parameterized, and see if i achieve a better outcome.  i would confess that i'm wondering whether HMC is able to handle joint sampling of the parameter space under a heavily parameterized (though identified and well-powered) model formulation.   I've always used HMC under analytic differentiation targeted to a sub-set of parameters inside a larger sequential scan sampling scheme.

I would welcome any other suggestions, if any occur to you.

Thanks for your time and help.  Terrance.

> The step size adaptation assumes that the accuracy of the Hamiltonian
> simulation can always be increased to an acceptable range by
> decreasing the step size. If this assumption is violated, then the
> adaptation absolutely will not converge. Models with reasonably smooth
> posteriors pretty much always satisfy this assumption. Numerical
> problems (e.g. from trying to invert near-singular matrices) and
> domain issues (e.g. from failing to constrain non-negative variables
> or positive-definite matrices) can cause it to be violated.
>
> My guess is that the adaptation failures will go away if the domain
> issues (s_m and s_d being unconstrained) and the  numerical issues
> (using matrix inversion instead of mdivide) people have brought up are

> Matt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] About DIC help.-
messages.body_plain:
We output the unnormalized log joint log probability
with each draw.  But not the log likelihood.

To calculate DIC with Stan, you'd need to
define the log likelihood as a generated quantity
and then compute DIC on the outside of Stan itself
once you have the log likelihood for each draw.

Depending on the demand for DIC-like calcs, we may make
it easier by allowing the model to specified explicitly
in terms of a prior block and a log likelihood block so that
we could output the log likelihood without the user having
to essentially define the model twice.

- Bob

messages.subject: best practice for estimating missing data
messages.subject_clean: best practice for estimating missing data
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

I am frequently faced with missing data.  Often, I need to use these data as predictors, so I need to find ways to estimate them.  Ideally, the estimation of missing values occurs in a way that does not feedback into the underlying probability model for which these data are being used.  In other words, the missing data are treated as an "observable function" or a type of "observed data".  I know how to do this in BUGS, and to a lesser extent in JAGS (see discussion here http://jackman.stanford.edu/blog/?p=1199), but the approach in STAN is still unclear to me.

I have tried to derive an example to demonstrate an application for this problem.  Attached is a R script that generates a dataset with missing values.  I've then followed a rather simplistic approach, where I fit a model to predict the observed data, use this model to estimate the missing values, and then patch together the missing and observed values into one vector to use as a predictor in another subsequent model.  What ends up happening is that I'm generating biased estimates, whereby I over-estimate the residual variance of my missing data (sigmaChb in the attached) and underestimate the effect of the predictor for the observed values (= lambda[1]).  I  guess that this is to be expected given the way I've written my model?...

My question is how would I write my model in STAN to get closer to the original "known" values that I used to create the original dataset?  Presumably, I would have to remove "chaob_miss_err" from the model block in the attached file, but sampling can't be done elsewhere.  Simply removing the residual error (chaob_miss_err) and dropping the missing values on the "mean" relationship doesn't address this problem either...

Again, thank you for your time, and particularly your patience with my questions.  I am an ecologist and have no formal training in statistics or computer science, so think of me as someone trying to speak a foreign language they learned by watching many re-runs of "Friends" on late-night TV.  I can communicate fairly well at this stage, but sometimes, things still get lost in translation.

Andrew

If you declare an otherwise unrestricted covariance matrix as a parameter, it will be positive definite with probability 1.0 (because it is really parameterized in terms of its Cholesky factor). For example,

parameters {
  cov_matrix[3] Sigma;
}

It gets tricky if you want a covariance matrix that has additional structure, but it is doable (and hopefully will be easy in Stan 2.0.x).

messages.body_plain:
On Saturday, October 6, 2012 5:02:21 PM UTC-4, atzap wrote:

> > This statement seems odd to me in that I think one virtue of (a future release of) Stan is that it would estimate the distribution of missing values in a way that is consistent with the probability model for which the data are being used. In other words, it would draw from the joint posterior distribution of the missing data and the unknown parameters. Otherwise, the estimates of the parameters would be biased, except under very restrictive assumptions about the missingness mechanism. However, the handling of missing values in the current version of Stan is not ideal, to be honest with you.
>

> But this isn't what is happening now though eh?...  Ultimately, I think I might be phrasing my question poorly.  Given the current handling of missing values, what is the best approach for recovering the original parameter estimates used to derive the data in my example?  My current attempts to model this in STAN lead to rather biased inference.

Stan is capable of doing what I would consider to be the right approach, but it is not particularly convenient to deal with missing data. In a real dataset, there is likely to be missingness scattered throughout several variables, so it is hard to just split the data up into observed blocks and missing blocks.

In your case, I believe that your .stan code is correct, but there was a bug in the R code that generated the data. In this line

bdat$y <- rbinom(bdat$N, bdat$n, plogis(-3 + .4 * bdat$chaob))

bdat$chaob is of length 20, while bdat$N is 120 and bdat$n is of length 120. What happens in these situations is that R "recycles" plogis(-3 + .4 * bdat$chaob) five times in order to provide 120 probabilities. In other words, the probabilities for the 20 observed data points are also being used for the 100 missing data points, which is inconsistent with the intended model.

If you change it to

bdat$y <- rbinom(bdat$N, bdat$n, plogis(-3 + .4 * chaob_act))

then, Stan seems to yield reasonable estimates. You can verify that the MLEs are close to what you intended with

mle <- glm(cbind(bdat$y, bdat$n - bdat$y) ~ chaob_act, family = binomial())
summary(mle)

These sorts of subtle bugs can be reduced by using odd numbers for sample sizes because recycling will trigger a warning.

Ben

The main thing that would speed it up is to
vectorize the normal() calls.  Even if you have to use
an intermediate array it'll be faster, but only
by a factor of 2--4 or so, not a factor
of 300.

Also, be sure to measure the effective sample size,
not just the number of draws.  It's easy to generate
gazillions of Metropolis draws quickly by choosing
a small proposal scale, but the effective sample size
will be lousy.

Do you know what algorithms mlwin and MCMCglmm use
for sampling?

Stan is at a disadvantage compared to systems that can exploit
sufficient statistics or calculate posteriors analytically as
can be done for many GLMs.

We're going to focus more on this kind of GLM in the
future for speed, but there's nothing on the horizon
immediately to look forward to.

- Bob

You can also specify -march=native in CXXFLAGS, but that won't make too much of a difference.

For large values of N and n2, the loop in your model{} block is going to take a while. For a model that can be estimated by Gibbs sampling, a Gibbs sampler can take less time than a HMC sampler per iteration, although hopefully Stan will require fewer iterations than would a Gibbs sampler to get a reasonable effective sample size. Hi Doug,

On Monday, October 8, 2012 11:32:24 AM UTC-4, Douglas Bates wrote:
> What tools are popular for the analysis and visualization of samples created by stan?  In particular, I would be interested in tools that use both lp__ and the parameter values.
>
> The manual mentions calculation of ESS, the effective sample size.  Are there convenient ways of assessing that, say in R?

If you use the rstan package, there are print and plot methods for the resulting stanfit object that do such things. As in

stopifnot(require(rstan))

schools_dat <- list(J = 8,
                    y = c(28,  8, -3,  7, -1,  1, 18, 12),
                    sigma = c(15, 10, 16, 11,  9, 11, 10, 18))

eight_schools <- stan(file = "http://wiki.stan.googlecode.com/git/rstangettingstarted/8schools.stan",
                      data = schools_dat)
print(eight_schools)
plot(eight_schools)

If you use command-line Stan, it just writes a .csv file, but at the moment, I think there is no convenience function to construct a stanfit object from the .csv files.

You can load library(mcmc), make a mcmc object from the .csv file, and and analyze it with their functions with

stopifnot(require(mcmc))
posterior <- as.mcmc(read.csv("samples.csv", comment.char = "#"))

Possibly also the library(boa).

Ben

messages.body_plain: I agree with Bob—vectorizing the normal() calls is the easiest thing to do, and could produce a very significant speedup. That's implemented below. Also, it's definitely not fair to just look at iterations—not all MCMC samples are created equal. One more way that the model could be sped up is by reparameterizing the model so that tau_u2 and u2 are decoupled in the prior, which is also implemented below. When you say something like tau ~ gamma(0.001, 0.001); u2[i] ~ normal(mu, 1/sqrt(tau)); the result is that 1. there is a very strong correlation in the prior (and often in the posterior) between tau and the elements of u2, which is undesirable because it demands small step sizes and 2. marginally u2[i] has a very, very heavy-tailed prior, which can result in a heavy-tailed posterior, which is more difficult for NUTS/HMC (and Gibbs, and Metropolis, and pretty much any MCMC algorithm) to sample from. You can instead say something like tau ~ gamma(0.001, 0.001); u2_z[i] ~ normal(mu, 1); u2[i] <- u2_z * 1/sqrt(tau); and sample on the space of the transformed variable u2_z instead of u2. This prior is equivalent to the one above, but u2_z is uncorrelated with tau (which is good) and has normal tails (which is also good). I've found that this sort of reparameterization can dramatically improve performance of hierarchical models. The model as written below should give a significant speedup, I think. (Assuming I didn't screw it up accidentally.) But again, please remember that what counts is the quality of the samples, not the total number of iterations. Matt data { int n2 ; int N ; real y[N] ; int school[N] ; } parameters { real u2_z[n2] ; // drawn from a standard normal real tau ; real tau_u2 ; // no periods in names real beta; // add bounds on the support of beta } transformed parameters { real u2[n2]; // this is the u2 you care about for (i in 1:n2) { u2[i] <- u2_z[i] * sqrt(1/tau_u2); } } model { real mu[N]; // should be vectorized real sigma; sigma <- sqrt(1/tau); # Level 1 definition for(i in 1:N) { mu[i] <- beta + u2[school[i]] ; // y[i] ~ normal(mu,sigma) ; // normal is parameterized in terms of the standard deviation } y ~ normal(mu, sigma); // vectorize instead of looping # level 2 definitions u2 ~ normal(0, sqrt(1/tau_u2)); // vectorize instead of looping where possible and use standard deviation # Priors for random terms // use gamma, rather than dgamma tau ~ gamma(0.001,0.001) ; tau_u2 ~ gamma(0.001,0.001) ; } On Mon, Oct 8, 2012 at 10:27 AM, Bob Carpenter wrote: > On 10/8/12 1:18 PM, Joe King wrote:> Hi Ben >> >> I have implemented your changes and the model now runs. >> >> However it seems to be very slow - so far it has taken about 30 mins for >> 1000 iterations (chain 1) and so far on chain 2 >> it has taken 40 mins and only reached 500 iterations..... I don't think I would call this model a GLM.  I would say it is a hierarchical linear model (MLM) or a linear mixed model (LMM).  One could refer to it as a generalized linear mixed model but only in the sense that all linear mixed models are also generalized linear mixed models.

I'm not sure how easy (well it is more a question of whether or not it is exceptionally difficult) it would be to extend the sampler framework to take advantage of models with a linear predictor expression like this.  Conditional on the values of sigma2 and sigma2.u2 the distribution of beta and mu is a multivariate normal and can be vectorized except that you really want to use a sparse model matrix, not a dense model matrix, when you get to large numbers of observations.

Not really.  The observed variance of the conditional means of the random effects (what are sometimes called the BLUPs, best linear unbiased estimators) that are available in an lmer fitted model as
ranef(myLmerModel)

On 10/8/12 11:32 AM, Douglas Bates wrote:

> interested in tools that use both lp__ and the parameter values.
>
> The manual mentions calculation of ESS, the effective sample size.  Are there convenient ways of assessing that, say in R?

Oops -- forgot to send this until I saw Ben's response.

RStan derives from Coda for analysis and R2WinBUGS and R2jags for
graphics.

The main difference is that Coda uses a slightly different
ESS estimator and a slightly different version of the Gelman
and Rubin R-hat convergence statistic.  Another minor diff
is that RStan shows the warmup samples as well as the
actual samples in the traceplots.

Another alternative that also provides Coda-like analysis
and R2WinBUGS-like graphing is mcmcplots by Curtis and Goldin.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: best practice for estimating missing data
messages.body_plain:
On 10/7/12 3:28 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> Stan is capable of doing what I would consider to be the right approach,

Basically the same thing as BUGS does -- use the joint
posterior with the missing data as "parameters".  You
need to model the missigness yourself, though, with data
missing completely at random being the baseline.

> but it is not particularly convenient to deal
> with missing data. In a real dataset, there is likely to be missingness scattered throughout several variables, so it is
> hard to just split the data up into observed blocks and missing blocks.

You can split each variable into observed and missing
components, put everything back together in a transformed
param, and you're good to go (though it's not the most
efficient approach imaginable).  You can do this variable
by variables, so rather than potentially 2^N missigness patterns
for N predictors, you only have to deal with N parameters.

Unfortunately, that's still N ugly index fiddles, which
wouldn't be that bad if they weren't so error-prone to
write and difficult to debug.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] About DIC help.-
messages.body_plain:
On 10/6/12 12:24 PM, Richard McElreath wrote:
> I'm attaching a working DIC computation example, comparing a multilevel model to a fixed model using DIC (reduces to AIC
> in fixed case). The deviance is calculated in the generated quantities block. Then I compute the expected parameter
> values outside of Stan and manually compute the deviance at the expectations.
>
> All Stan would really need to do to make this easy would be provide for a final calculation of generated quantities at
> the expected values of the trace. But that would just be a convenience.
>
> I'm personally torn on whether software should make these metrics easy or not. On the one hand, all of these metrics
> (DIC/WAIC) are flawed. On the other hand, ignoring over fitting can be worse.

I have no opinion on DIC.

The reason we can't automate the calculation of
the log likelihood is that the Stan model isn't
neatly divided into a likelihood and prior component.

If we split the model into two blocks, then we could
calculate the log likelihood (and log prior and log joint)
without measurable extra cost and without extra code in the generated
quantities block.

I believe our jury (i.e., Andrew) is still out on what
to do, so we've been holding off building in that kind of
thing.

One issue on the horizon is that we're imagining writing
compound models that have priors and likelihood in one
function call.  That would get in the way of splitting out
the likelihood calc unless we did something fancier.

- Bob

messages.subject: [stan-users] DIC talk
messages.body_plain:
I'm not thrilled with DIC but I don't know if we have any better alternatives right now.  There are 3 difficulties with computing DIC in Stan.  The first, as Bob noted, is that to compute DIC, the user would need to flag which parts of the unnormalized joint density go into the "likelihood."  There's no automatic way of doing this; it depends not just on the model but on the purposes for which it will be used.  But, not only is there no automatic way to identify these lines of code, in Stan there's no way to do it by hand.  This is the problem Bob was pointing out:  we would have to alter Stan to allow the user to flag the appropriate lines in the code.  The third difficulty with implementing DIC is that it requires computation of the log likelihood given the posterior mean of the parameters.  This requires computation of the mean and feeding it back into the calculation (also it requires some help if the likelihood is undefined at the posterior mean of theta, which in turn is one reason I'm not thrilled with DIC.

A

On Oct 8, 2012, at 3:44 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

>
>
> On 10/6/12 12:24 PM, Richard McElreath wrote:
>> I'm attaching a working DIC computation example, comparing a multilevel model to a fixed model using DIC (reduces to AIC
>> in fixed case). The deviance is calculated in the generated quantities block. Then I compute the expected parameter
>> values outside of Stan and manually compute the deviance at the expectations.
>>
>> All Stan would really need to do to make this easy would be provide for a final calculation of generated quantities at
>> the expected values of the trace. But that would just be a convenience.
>>
>> I'm personally torn on whether software should make these metrics easy or not. On the one hand, all of these metrics
>> (DIC/WAIC) are flawed. On the other hand, ignoring over fitting can be worse.
>
> I have no opinion on DIC.
>
> The reason we can't automate the calculation of
> the log likelihood is that the Stan model isn't
> neatly divided into a likelihood and prior component.
>
> If we split the model into two blocks, then we could
> calculate the log likelihood (and log prior and log joint)
> without measurable extra cost and without extra code in the generated
> quantities block.
>
> I believe our jury (i.e., Andrew) is still out on what
> to do, so we've been holding off building in that kind of
> thing.
>
> One issue on the horizon is that we're imagining writing
> compound models that have priors and likelihood in one
> function call.  That would get in the way of splitting out
> the likelihood calc unless we did something fancier.
>
> - Bob
>

> --
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Douglas

Yes ! I can make the data available, because I simulated it myself. I shall post it here, below, but first I would like to explain a little about it so you can understand what I did.

In my "real-life" data (which I have not analysed with stan yet) I have observations on pupils, nested in schools. There is 1 observation per pupil in the data. Moreover, the data are over several years. Interest is centred on how the school-level random effects have changed over time.

So, I simulated 3 years worth of data, where each year had a different variance for the school-level effects and I wanted to be able to "get back" those different variances in my model. I was able to do that very well, using lme4 with this:

lmer(outcome ~1 + (year|school.ID),data=dt.all)

So my ultimate goal is to run a model with stan which does the same. But first I am just trying out the simple variance components model, for which I gave the output for earlier.

So, this is the code that generates the data:

set.seed(10)
n.schools <- 100
n.pupils <- n.schools^2

pupil.ID <- seq(1,n.pupils,1)     # pupils with unique IDs
school.ID <- 1+trunc((pupil.ID-1)/n.schools) # schools with unique IDs
school.effect <- rnorm(n.schools,0,1)  # school-level effects, SD=1
outcome <- numeric(n.pupils)
for (i in 1:n.pupils) {
    outcome[i] <- 20+school.effect[school.ID[i]]+rnorm(1,0,5)
}

dt.y1 <- as.data.frame(cbind(pupil.ID, school.ID, outcome))

# Year 2
dt.y1$year <- rep(2004,n.pupils)  # year ID for first period

pupil.ID <- seq(n.pupils+1,n.pupils*2,1)     # add more pupils with unique IDs
school.effect <- rnorm(n.schools,0,4)  # school-level effects - SD=4
for (i in 1:n.pupils) {
    outcome[i] <- 20+school.effect[school.ID[i]]+rnorm(1,0,5)
}
dt.y2 <- as.data.frame(cbind(pupil.ID, school.ID, outcome))
dt.y2$year <- rep(2005,n.pupils)  # year ID for first period

# Year 3

pupil.ID <- seq((n.pupils*2)+1,n.pupils*3,1)     # add more pupils with unique IDs
school.effect <- rnorm(n.schools,0,16)  # school-level effects, SD=16
for (i in 1:n.pupils) {
    outcome[i] <- 20+school.effect[school.ID[i]]+rnorm(1,0,5)
}
dt.y3 <- as.data.frame(cbind(pupil.ID, school.ID, outcome))
dt.y3$year <- rep(2006,n.pupils)  # year ID for first period

fit.lme4.y1 <- lmer(outcome ~1 + (1|school.ID),data=dt.y1)
summary(fit.lme4.y1)

fit.lme4.y2 <- lmer(outcome ~1 + (1|school.ID),data=dt.y2)
summary(fit.lme4.y2)

fit.lme4.y3 <- lmer(outcome ~1 + (1|school.ID),data=dt.y3)
summary(fit.lme4.y3)

dt.all <- rbind(dt.y1,dt.y2,dt.y3)
fit.lme4.all.1 <- lmer(outcome ~1 + (1|school.ID),data=dt.all)
summary(fit.lme4.all.1)

dt.all$year <- as.factor(dt.all$year)
fit.lme4.all.2 <- lmer(outcome ~1 + (year|school.ID),data=dt.all)
summary(fit.lme4.all.2)

Thanks !
JK

>> We don't really recommend Stan for models like LDA.

>>
>> That being the case, you might as well go for an optimizer.
>> Like the very scalable online one Matt (the inventor of
>> our sampler, NUTS) wrote for Vowpal Wabbit:
>>
>>    http://hunch.net/~vw/
>>
>> and described in this paper:
>>
>>    http://www.cs.princeton.edu/~blei/papers/HoffmanBleiBach2010b.pdf
>>
>> The reason Stan's consuming so much memory is that we're
>> building up the log probability expression tree in memory to
>> use to compute auto-diff.
>>
>> I believe PyMC uses Metropolis, which may run and provide
>> samples, but isn't going to give you very efficient sampling,
>> even around a single mode.
>>
>> Finally, the Stan model isn't well formed because
>> we don't do integer sampling.  So the "topic ~ categorical(...)"
>> isn't going to do what you think -- what it will do is
>> add log categorical(topic|theta[i]) to the log probabilty
>> where topic is uninitialized.
>>
>> What you need to do is marginalize out the discrete
>> variables because Stan doesn't sample them.  Here's
>> a note on how to do that for basic LDA:
>>
>> http://lingpipe-blog.com/2011/04/14/summing-out-topic-assignments-ld/
>>
>> This can also be a useful move if you're applying some
>> kind of optimization.
>>
>>
>>> model {
>>> int start;
>>> int topic;
>>> for (n in 1:K) {
>>> psi[n] ~ dirichlet(beta[n]);
>>> }
>>> for (n in 1:D) {
>>> theta[n] ~ dirichlet(alpha);
>>> }
>>> start <- 1;
>>> for (i in 1:D) {
>>>    for (j in start:doc_ind[i] - 1) {
>>>      topic ~ categorical(theta[i]);
>>>      words[j] ~ categorical(psi[topic + 1]);
>>>    }
>>>    start <- doc_ind[i];
>>> }
>>> }
>>
>> Also, I don't follow the use of start here.  Why not
>> write this loop as in the Blei et al. LDA paper?  That is,
>> as:
>>
>> for (d in 1:D) {
>>    theta[d] ~ dirichlet(alpha);

> On Monday, October 8, 2012 9:29:05 PM UTC+1, Andrew Gelman wrote:
 >
 >     You've heard this before from me, but I'll say it again:  I think gamma(.001,.001) is bad news.

On 10/8/12 5:09 PM, Joe King wrote:
> In another project I had problems with gamma(.001,.001) using MCMCglmm and instead I used a parameter-expanded
> representation of a half-cauchy priory with better results. Do you think that would be appropriate here ? Unfortunately
> I didn't fully understand how the the scaling worked.

You can read up on Andrew's full set of recommendations here:

   Bayesian Analysis (2006) 1, Number 3, pp. 515ï¿½533
   Prior distributions for variance parameters in
   hierarchical models
   Andrew Gelman

   http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/taumain.pdf

We've been using half-Cauchy distributions for deviations and
full Cauchy for regression coefficients.  In
Stan, you don't even need to truncate because we only need
the probability up to a proportion.  So you could replace this:

 > tau ~ gamma(0.001, 0.001);
 > u2_z[i] ~ normal(mu, 1);
 > u2[i] <- u2_z * 1/sqrt(tau);

with a proper z-score and a prior directly on deviation:

   sigma ~ cauchy(0,5);
   u2_z[i] ~ normal(0,1);
   u2[i] <- mu + u2_z[i] * sigma;

I also pulled mu out for reasons Matt outlined in previous
messages (and which is going into the next manual).

Because Stan doesn't exploit conjugacy, the Cauchy will
be roughly the same efficiency per iteration as the gamma
prior.

Our standard advice to do some sensitivity analysis also
stands -- if you don't want the prior to have a big effect,
make sure it doesn't by testing alternatives.

- Bob

The default in Stan is to adapt step size during warmup,
but then to use a fixed step size in sampling.  So you
see the same step size in every sample.

If you use the varying step command-line flag, epsilon_pm,
you get different step sizes per iteration.  The "_pm" is
missing from the doc in the manual, so I just fixed that.
Here's how it should read:

Model execution option (page 23 or so of the manual):

--epsilon_pm=<[0,1]>
   Sample epsilon uniformly from the interval
   [epsilon * (1 - epsilon_pm), epsilon * (1 + epsilon_pm)]
   (default = 0.0)

- Bob

> Never mind about that hypothesis I mentioned.

> The reason for the slow mixing we're seeing is pretty basic—in this

> instead of alpha?) is very highly anti-correlated with the
> school-level effects u2. On average, the posterior correlation is

One way around this is to sample from the coefficient vector, which in this case can be orthogonalized.  In general the conditional distribution of coefficients, even in the case of mixed-effects models can be orthogonalized.

IIRC JAGS has a specialized sampler for this.

I'm not sure how difficult it would be but the ability to use sparse matrices, which are supported in Eigen and RcppEigen, would be very helpful here.

For the record, I would use something like
library(lme4)
library(rstan)

set.seed(1234321)
samp <- within(data.frame(schoolID=gl(300,100)),
               outcome <- 20 + rnorm(30000, sd=10) + rnorm(300,sd=5)[schoolID])
(lm1 <- lmer(outcome ~ 1|schoolID, samp))
## The next line can only be run with the development lme4 installed as
## install.packages("lme4", repos="http://R-forge.R-project.org")
densityplot(pr1 <- profile(lm1), ylab=NULL, layout=c(3,1))

schools_code <- '
  data {
    int<lower=1> N;                   // number of observations
    int<lower=1> J;                   // number of schools
    int<lower=1,upper=J> school[N];   // school for each obs
    real         y[N];          // observed outcome
  }
  parameters {
    real mu;
    real<lower=0> sigma;
    real<lower=0> sigma1;
    real eta[J];
  }
  model {
    real mm[N];

    for (i in 1:N)

      mm[i] <- mu + eta[school[i]];

    y   ~ normal(mm, sigma);
    eta ~ normal(0, sigma1);

    sigma ~ gamma(0.001000,0.001000) ;
    sigma1 ~ gamma(0.001000,0.001000) ;
  }
'

fit <- stan(model_name="schools", model_code=schools_code,
            data=with(samp, list(N=nrow(samp), J=length(levels(schoolID)),
            y=outcome, school=as.integer(schoolID))),
            iter = 1000, chains = 4)

messages.subject: integer arithmetic in Stan may not do what you expect
messages.subject_clean: integer arithmetic in Stan may not do what you expect
messages.body_plain:
Andrew's been using Stan in his Bayesian Data Analysis
class, and a student brought up this issue:

 >> When I am doing Computing problem (b), I used nu ~ exponential(1/10) as a prior and the program cannot work, then I
 >> tried nu ~ exponential(0.1) and it works... What is the difference?

We use standard IEEE arithmetic (as in C++ or Java), where
integer divisions like (1/10) round down to 0.  If you want floating
point division, you need to write (1.0 / 10.0) instead.

I should probably put something in the model translator
to warn users who try to divide integers by integers, as
that's going to be the main source of problems.

This is in the manual and in the differences from BUGS appendix.
We're trying to not overload the getting-started examples too much.

- Bob

messages.subject: Parallel chains
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

It occurs to me that the computation of multiple chains is an
embarrassingly parallel problem (at least, according to my beginner's
understanding of MCMC). Has any thought been put into parallelizing
chain computation in stan for systems with more than one core (i.e.
most modern systems)? I had a try at using the doMC interface to
parallelism in R for unix machines (I'm on Mac OS X) and posted the
code here:

https://gist.github.com/3861998

On my machine (1.8GHz Core i7), I get about 2x speedup using the
parallel approach. Not the full 4x speedup I might have naively
expected from my 4-core machine, but still a worthwhile improvement.
(Of course, the example is on the order of seconds in duration, so
"worthwhile" is debatable; I'll run some more computationally
intensive examples overnight to see how this scales.) Possibly deeper
integration of parallelism in stan/rstan might eliminate redundancies
and/or overhead to achieve further improvements?

I also notice that it appears that the "verbose=FALSE" argument to
stan() doesn't actually do anything...

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology
Dalhousie University

Looking to arrange a meeting? Check my public calendar: http://goo.gl/BYH99

~ Certainty is folly... I think. ~

We have talked about it. Implementing parallel chains in stan() via the parallel library or the doMC library would not be too difficult on Linux or a Mac because in those cases the R process is simply forked. But that route is not available on Windows. The parallel engines that do work on Windows start entirely new R processes, which is a challenge for rstan (or anything that relies on the inline package) because the executable generated by stan() somehow needs to be dynamically loaded into these new R processes.

> I'm also interested in the possibility of using the CUDA architecture:
> my GPU has 96 cores with 1GB shared RAM : does anyone have any thoughts
> on this ?

There have been a variety of efforts to get R working with GPUs; see for example

http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/OpenCL/index.html

But Stan has only been tested on Intel CPUs so far.

Ben

> Hi Doug,
>
> On Tuesday, October 9, 2012 5:49:17 PM UTC-4, Douglas Bates wrote:
> > Thanks for the suggestions, Ben.
> >
> > I have a couple of style questions, mostly related to the need to specify the length of vectors in addition to the vectors themselves.  It is common to have stanzas like
> > data {
> >    int<lower=1> N;
> >    real<lower=0> rate[N];
> >    real<lower=0> conc[N];
> > }
> > in a stan model (although sometimes in the manuals the declaration of N is "int<lower=0> N;", which doesn't make sense to me as you can't really expect to do much with 0-length vectors).
>

I wasn't clear apparently.  What I was pointing out is that it doesn't make sense to me to have a lower bound of 0 on N, which is one of the dimensions of the data in the model.  In some cases dimensions of zero make sense as the edge condition but for an McMC model you probably need a non-zero number of data points.  It's a trivial matter and probably not worth further discussion.

> I can see how this would be confusing from an R perspective where almost everything is a vector in some sense, but some vectors happen to be of length one. But from a C++ perspective, N is a scalar while rate and conc are std::vectors. In other words, the above parses as:
>
> class doug_model : public prob_grad_ad {
> private:
>     int N;
>     vector<double> rate;
>     vector<double> conc;
> public:
> ...
>
> I suppose it is valid to write in a .stan file
>

I realize that N is needed in the C++ code, I am just advocating trying to find a way to make it easier to specify it in R when using rstan.

> data {
>   int<lower=0> N[1];
> }
>
> to get a std::vector called N of length 1. But it isn't necessary and you would have to remember to write N[1] subsequently. We put some effort into making Stan "work" with 0-length vectors and 0x0 matrices. But I wouldn't rely on it working, and I can't think of a situation where it wasn't a mistake on the user's part.
>
> > When passing data from R and even when reading data from an R dump file you determine the length of the vector as part of the parsing of the arguments.  Is it reasonable to try to find a way to avoid needing to specify the vector lengths so that a data.frame can be passed as the data?  In my example I take advantage of the fact that a data frame is also a list and use the c(<data.frame>, N=nrow(frm)) construction to get the vectors and their length into a list.  Of course, it would not be difficult to write a short R function to do that packaging of the vectors and their length but it seems like it should be possible to finesse that issue.
>
> It sounds like a reasonable request, but I'm not immediately seeing how to make it work on the C++ side. Maybe the C++ file stan() generates could #define NROW__  and let this .stan syntax
>
> data {
>   real<lower=0> rate[]; // implicitly using NROW__ as the length
>   real<lower=0> conc[]; // implicitly using NROW__ as the length
> }
>
> be valid. Andrew would probably like it and Bob would probably hate it. We'll see.
>
> > One point on terminology, although it is probably too late to change this and it may be a holdover from the BUGS/JAGS world, you recommend the .Rdata extension for files in the R dump format.  Typically in R the .Rdata extension is used for binary save files, not R dump files.  This could end up being confusing.
>
> This is confusing. In Appendix D.3, footnote 2, of the Stan manual we note this confusion, but I can't remember if there was a reason we use .Rdata in the examples.
>
> Ben
>

This is the right edge behavior if zero-length data results
in the parameters being sampled from the prior.  But if
the model specifies an operation only defined on non-empty
vectors, such as mean or sd, then the model will raise an
error if there's a zero-length input, so it'd be better to
catch the error early by putting it in the data declaration.

> I realize that N is needed in the C++ code, I am just advocating trying to find a way to make it easier to specify it in
> R when using rstan.

Andrew was saying exactly the same thing.  And
also advocating writing a reader for (multiple joined)
files CSV data, which would be very helpful in
the typical (multilevel) regression setting.

Any suggestions on how we could figure out what N
should be?  The way all the readers are set up in C++,
we need to know the length of vectors to read.  (The
underlying reason is the conversion from the unconstrained
parameter vector to the constrained parameters used in
the model.)

>
>     to get a std::vector called N of length 1. But it isn't necessary and you would have to remember to write N[1]
>     subsequently. We put some effort into making Stan "work" with 0-length vectors and 0x0 matrices. But I wouldn't rely
>     on it working, and I can't think of a situation where it wasn't a mistake on the user's part.
>
>         When passing data from R and even when reading data from an R dump file you determine the length of the vector
>         as part of the parsing of the arguments.  Is it reasonable to try to find a way to avoid needing to specify the
>         vector lengths so that a data.frame can be passed as the data?  In my example I take advantage of the fact that
>         a data frame is also a list and use the c(<data.frame>, N=nrow(frm)) construction to get the vectors and their
>         length into a list.  Of course, it would not be difficult to write a short R function to do that packaging of
>         the vectors and their length but it seems like it should be possible to finesse that issue.
>
>
>     It sounds like a reasonable request, but I'm not immediately seeing how to make it work on the C++ side. Maybe the
>     C++ file stan() generates could #define NROW__  and let this .stan syntax
>
>     |
>     data {
>        real<lower=0> rate[]; // implicitly using NROW__ as the length
>        real<lower=0> conc[]; // implicitly using NROW__ as the length
>     }
>     |
>
>     be valid. Andrew would probably like it and Bob would probably hate it. We'll see.

I'll reserve judgment until I can figure out how
something like this could be made to work!

I have no issue with the language doing more inference
on data structures and types as long as it's well defined and
not too confusing (like I don't think we should go to C++-style
template metaprogramming!).

You might be able to use something like rate_len and conc_len,
but then we lose the constraint that they're the same length.
I want that to be declared in the data in the model.  I believe
it makes the models easier to read because the bounds of all
the data structures are right there.

It can be a bit more of a pain to get a model working, but
I also believe it pays the cost back in debugging effort.

Other people have very different preferences for typing in
their programming languages.  I hear some people even like Perl
and Python and R programming :-)

>     This is confusing. In Appendix D.3, footnote 2, of the Stan manual we note this confusion, but I can't remember if
>     there was a reason we use .Rdata in the examples.

Fixing this is on the to-do list -- the footnote's a stop-gap.
This was my fault for not understanding the R conventions.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Parallel chains
messages.body_plain:
Chad Scherer's Passage sampler does within-chain
parallelism in Gibbs sampling by figuring out
independent blocks.  (It also compiles to C++.)
HMC's a little trickier here -- we'd need to figure
out how to parallelize our log probability calcs.

But Stan is very much like a general-purpose
imperative program in its implementation.  It is
strongly typed like Fortran, so there are some things
with loops we could probably do soundly.

We're going to start with simple parallel chains.
We just discussed this in our meeting yesterday and
think we can roll out for Linux/Mac through R pretty
easily, but not so much on Windows.

I'm not so clear on how we could parallelize a single chain
in Stan.  Even if we had a parallel matrix lib for
some operations, there's an issue with the re-entrancy
of our auto-dif across threads (we use thread local
to synch if necessary, and that won't work if we
add multiple cores per thread).

Parallelizing with things like GPUs in R doesn't
help.  First, GPUs are a pain and only work on
32-bit vectorized ops, which is just not how Stan's
layed out.  Second, speeding up R doesn't help because
Stan's written in C++.  Within epsilon, all the
time is spent in compiling the Stan program and
executing the C++.

- Bob

> make: *** [bin/stan/command/stanc.o] Error 1

My first guess with all of these is that the machine ran out of memory. You can watch memory consumption while it is compiling with Task Manager. It may be possible to increase what I believe is called "virtual memory" in Windows XP and is called a "swap file" by everyone else.

You can also try to throttle back on the optimization. Although we recommend that *models* be compiled at O3, whether the *parser* is compiled with optimization doesn't make much difference. So, maybe

$ make O=2 bin/stanc.exe

works, and if not then try O=1 and O=0. Although a while back, we were having a problem where the parser would build with higher levels of optimization but not lower levels. My guess is that you will run into more problems later. But this might get you one step closer and you may be able to do some models.

We don't test regularly on Windows XP or any 32bit system, although Jiqiang did get Stan to build on his Windows XP laptop a few months ago.

Ben

messages.subject: slow sampling of a SEM
messages.body_plain:
I having been trying Stan as an alternative to JAGS, where the structural equation models (SEMs) that I frequently fit can take 3 weeks to run!  This might sound like I'm doing something wrong, but colleagues of mine have similar run times (unless we're both do something blatantly wrong...).  Our datasets are not particularly large ('000s of observations), but the models seem to be intense computationally.

I have been trying to fit a Stan model to one of these SEMs, which only has about 200 observations (see attached, includes link to data).  It has taken a bit longer than a day to run 70,000 iterations, and I still haven't hit convergence.  I've gone over my code several times now and am a bit stuck as to where the efficiencies lie...  The painful centering step is included because I eventually want to standardize my parameters to a mean of 0 and sd of 1 to compare their relative effects.  But, the sd step is problematic (see https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups=#!topic/stan-users/cYjRmPY4k4E), so has been omitted for now.

Essentially, in this example, I have counts of three types of animals (denoted by y, y2, and y3) and I want to model their relative abundance, measured in different lakes and across years.  For one group, y, we want to model their abundance as a function of an unobserved latent variable called food availability.  This is affected by abundances of the other two groups of animals (y2 and y3), and is related to "phyto" densities.  Finally, we also want to model the effects of predation on y2 and y3, but many of the predator densities are unobserved, so we "impute" these given a separate regression.  I'm afraid that I can't provide a "simple" model for this particular problem - the slow sampling is very much context dependent.  Furthermore, many of the models I try to fit are complex and messy.  That is the reality of applying these methods in my field.

So I guess my convoluted question is how can I make Stan run faster?  This is being asked a few times now, so perhaps worth a FAQ post...  But, I am trying to do the obvious here, i.e. vectorize and minimize operations within loops, and I have optimized my C++ compiler as per the RStan Getting Started guide <http://code.google.com/p/stan/wiki/RStanGettingStarted#Modify_C++_compiler_optimization_level>.

Perhaps Stan can't / won't run faster for this particular class of problems?  I guess I was hoping that I would get 5-10X speed ups relative to JAGS (as found by others for their problems https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups=#!searchin/stan-users/richard$20faster/stan-users/-_cVwdGgoqs/SKHN7yc8oCgJ).  Stan seems to get closer to convergence in fewer iterations than JAGS, but each iteration takes longer, especially when you can't run chains in parallel (which I do in JAGS).  For the record, I've been testing Stan on a pretty slow machine (2.2 Ghz).  I hope to get it running on my much faster 3.4 Ghz quad-core shortly.  Perhaps running it on there, with a chain on each core, and then merging the results afterwards, might be the best bet at this stage?  Again, would appreciate any thoughts on the topic.  I've just lived with the slowness of JAGS for too long and was hoping Stan would provide a great leap forward.  In fact, things are so slow to converge, I wonder whether we can even fit these models within the context of standard Bayesian packages...

Thanks again for your time. I realize that the questions are probably starting to get pretty repetitive at this stage, and more are arriving every day.  Hopefully the rest of us "users" can contribute more once we understand things better.

- Andrew
