On Oct 12, 2012, at 12:14 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:

> Good news everyone (particularly people who are willing to help us test)! Jiqiang wrote a function that will be included in rstan 1.0.3 that facilitates running chains in parallel. In particular, you can do something like
>

> stopifnot(require(rstan))
>
> schools_dat <- list(J = 8,
>                     y = c(28,  8, -3,  7, -1,  1, 18, 12),
>                     sigma = c(15, 10, 16, 11,  9, 11, 10, 18))
>
> eight_schools <- stan(file = "http://wiki.stan.googlecode.com/git/rstangettingstarted/8schools.stan",
>                       data = schools_dat, iter = 1, chains = 1) # just get it to compile the model
>
> library(

> parallel) # or some other parallelizing package

>
> chains <- 8
>
> posterior <- mclapply(1:chains, mc.cores = chains, FUN = function(chain) { # or another parallelizing function

>
>                stan(fit = eight_schools, data = schools_dat, chains = 1, verbose = FALSE, refresh = -1)
>              })
>
> posterior <- sflist2stanfit(posterior) # see below for function definition
> print(posterior)
> plot(posterior)

>
> where the necessary new function sflist2stanfit() is defined at the end of this post and is also attached.
>
> Some things to note. In the example above, I first ran the eight schools model for one iteration of one chain just to get the code to compile. Then I passed that eight_schools object to the fit argument of stan() in each of the eight chains (with the defaults for warmup, iter, etc.). This route avoids having to recompile the code eight times and will work for mclapply() in the parallel package, which executes the function locally on a multicore machine. Note that mclapply() does not do anything in parallel on Windows, so you need to use an alternative parallelizing library / function in that case.
>
> This route will probably not work if you are using the snow package or a similar package to execute the chains on a remote server because the remote server will not know what to do with the code compiled on your laptop. In that case, you would need to specify file or model_code rather than fit, so that the remote server would compile the code for each chain. Also, if file is a filepath on your laptop, the remote server will not be able to access it, so you would need to upload your .stan file to a readable directory on the remote server and specify file accordingly. Similarly, the data somehow need to be available on the remote server and the remote server obviously needs to have rstan installed and loaded. Note that stanfit objects can be quite large in size, so you could be pulling GB of uncompressed data from the remote server to your laptop at the end.
>
> If you have access to some sort of computer lab with a bunch of physical PCs that have rstan but are not networked, you could execute stan() with chains = 1 on each PC, save the  resulting stanfit object to a USB stick with something like save(chain_3, file = "chain_3.RData", compress = "xz"), use the load() command to load each .RData object onto a common machine, put them into a list, and use sflist2stanfit() to consolidate them into a stanfit object that can be analyzed by the tools in the rstan package. Note that each chain needs to be given a different object name to avoid them overwriting each other when you load() them onto the common machine.
>
> For the high-performance (including parallel) capabilities that are available in R or R packages, execute help(package = parallel) in R or see
>
> http://cran.r-project.org/web/views/HighPerformanceComputing.html
>
> Ben (but mostly Jiqiang)
>
> P.S. The new function below can be pasted in now but is now defined in the rstan tree at the end of
>
> https://code.google.com/p/stan/source/browse/rstan/rstan/R/stanfit-class.R
>
> sflist2stanfit <- function(sflist) {
>   # merge a list of stanfit objects into one
>   # Args:
>   #   sflist, a list of stanfit objects, each element of which
>   #   should have equal length of `iter`, `warmup`, and `thin`.
>   # Returns:
>   #   A new stanfit objects have all the chains in each element of sf_list.
>   #   The date would be where the new object is created.
>   # Note:
>   #   * method get_seed would not work well for this merged
>   #     stanfit object. But all the information is still there.
>   #   * When print function is called, the sampler is obtained
>   #     only from the first chain.
>   #
>   sf_len <- length(sflist)
>   if (sf_len < 2) stop("'sflist' should have more than 1 elements")
>   if (!is.list(sflist) ||
>       any(sapply(sflist, function(x) !is(x, "stanfit")))) {
>     stop("'sflist' must be a list of 'stanfit' objects")
>   }
>   if (any(sapply(sflist, function(x) x@mode != 0))) {
>     stop("each 'stanfit' object in 'sflist' must contain samples")
>   }
>   for (i in 2:sf_len) {
>     if (!identical(sflist[[i]]@sim$pars_oi, sflist[[1]]@sim$pars_oi) ||
>         !identical(sflist[[i]]@sim$dims_oi, sflist[[1]]@sim$dims_oi))
>       stop("parameters in element ", i, " (stanfit object) is different from in element 1")
>     if (sflist[[i]]@sim$n_save[1] != sflist[[1]]@sim$n_save[1] ||
>         sflist[[i]]@sim$warmup2[1] != sflist[[1]]@sim$warmup2[1])
>       stop("all 'stanfit' objects should have equal length of iterations and warmup")
>   }
>   n_chains = sum(sapply(sflist, function(x) x@sim$chains))
>   sim = list(samples = do.call(c, lapply(sflist, function(x) x@sim$samples)),
>              chains = n_chains,
>              iter = sflist[[1]]@sim$iter,
>              thin = sflist[[1]]@sim$thin,
>              warmup = sflist[[1]]@sim$warmup,
>              n_save = rep(sflist[[1]]@sim$n_save[1], n_chains),
>              warmup2 = rep(sflist[[1]]@sim$warmup2[1], n_chains),
>              thin = rep(sflist[[1]]@sim$thin[1], n_chains),
>              permutation = do.call(c, lapply(sflist, function(x) x@sim$permutation)),
>              pars_oi = sflist[[1]]@sim$pars_oi,
>              dims_oi = sflist[[1]]@sim$dims_oi,
>              fnames_oi = sflist[[1]]@sim$fnames_oi,
>              n_flatnames = sflist[[1]]@sim$n_flatnames)
>   nfit <- new("stanfit",
>               model_name = sflist[[1]]@model_name,
>               model_pars = sflist[[1]]@model_pars,
>               par_dims  = sflist[[1]]@par_dims,
>               mode = 0L,
>               sim = sim,
>               inits = do.call(c, lapply(sflist, function(x) x@inits)),
>               stan_args = do.call(c, lapply(sflist, function(x) x@stan_args)),
>               stanmodel = sflist[[1]]@stanmodel,
>               date = date(),
>               .MISC = new.env())
>   invisible(nfit)
> }
>

>

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

For the lazy people out there, here is a convenient function that wraps up things from Andrew:

stanParallel <- function(fit=NULL, chains=4, ...) {
    args <- list(...)
    args$chains <- 1

    ## if fit is given, then use the compiled code from there
    if(is.null(fit)) {
        targs <- args
        targs$iter <- 1
        fit <- do.call(stan, targs)
    }

    args$file <- NULL
    args$fit <- fit
    args$refresh <- -1
    args$verbose <- FALSE

    posterior <- mclapply(1:chains, FUN = function(chain) do.call(stan, args) )

    posterior <- sflist2stanfit(posterior) # see below for function definition

    invisible(posterior)
}

Just worked like a charm for me.

One side note: You have to use the mc.cores option to set the number of cores to use, i.e. put a options(mc.cores=2) in your .Rprofile .

Best,

Sebastian

I failed to mention something potentially important. In code such this:

On Friday, October 12, 2012 2:41:30 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
>     posterior <- mclapply(1:chains, FUN = function(chain) do.call(stan, args) )

It is important to pass chain_id=chain to Stan, as in

posterior <- mclapply(1:chains, FUN = function(chain) {
               args$chain_id <- chain
               do.call(stan, args)
             })

rstan does not use R's pseduo random number generators; rather Stan's uses one of Boost's PRNGs. I'm still not convinced that what we are doing is optimal, but setting chain_id causes Stan to make some effort to ensure that the chains start at interspersed points in the period of the PRNG.

messages.subject: Parallel chains now supported (sort of)
messages.body_plain:
Good news everyone (particularly people who are willing to help us test)! Jiqiang wrote a function that will be included in rstan 1.0.3 that facilitates running chains in parallel. In particular, you can do something like

stopifnot(require(rstan))

schools_dat <- list(J = 8,
                    y = c(28,  8, -3,  7, -1,  1, 18, 12),
                    sigma = c(15, 10, 16, 11,  9, 11, 10, 18))

eight_schools <- stan(file = "http://wiki.stan.googlecode.com/git/rstangettingstarted/8schools.stan",
                      data = schools_dat, iter = 1, chains = 1) # just get it to compile the model

library(parallel) # or some other parallelizing package
chains <- 8

posterior <- mclapply(1:chains, mc.cores = chains, FUN = function(chain) { # or another parallelizing function
               stan(fit = eight_schools, data = schools_dat, chains = 1, verbose = FALSE, refresh = -1, chain_id=chain)
             })

posterior <- sflist2stanfit(posterior) # see below for function definition
print(posterior)
plot(posterior)

where the necessary new function sflist2stanfit() is defined at the end of this post and is also attached.

Some things to note. In the example above, I first ran the eight schools model for one iteration of one chain just to get the code to compile. Then I passed that eight_schools object to the fit argument of stan() in each of the eight chains (with the defaults for warmup, iter, etc.). This route avoids having to recompile the code eight times and will work for mclapply() in the parallel package, which executes the function locally on a multicore machine. Note that mclapply() does not do anything in parallel on Windows, so you need to use an alternative parallelizing library / function in that case.

This route will probably not work if you are using the snow package or a similar package to execute the chains on a remote server because the remote server will not know what to do with the code compiled on your laptop. In that case, you would need to specify file or model_code rather than fit, so that the remote server would compile the code for each chain. Also, if file is a filepath on your laptop, the remote server will not be able to access it, so you would need to upload your .stan file to a readable directory on the remote server and specify file accordingly. Similarly, the data somehow need to be available on the remote server and the remote server obviously needs to have rstan installed and loaded. Note that stanfit objects can be quite large in size, so you could be pulling GB of uncompressed data from the remote server to your laptop at the end.

If you have access to some sort of computer lab with a bunch of physical PCs that have rstan but are not networked, you could execute stan() with chains = 1 on each PC, save the  resulting stanfit object to a USB stick with something like save(chain_3, file = "chain_3.RData", compress = "xz"), use the load() command to load each .RData object onto a common machine, put them into a list, and use sflist2stanfit() to consolidate them into a stanfit object that can be analyzed by the tools in the rstan package. Note that each chain needs to be given a different object name to avoid them overwriting each other when you load() them onto the common machine.

For the high-performance (including parallel) capabilities that are available in R or R packages, execute help(package = parallel) in R or see

http://cran.r-project.org/web/views/HighPerformanceComputing.html

Ben (but mostly Jiqiang)

P.S. The new function below can be pasted in now but is now defined in the rstan tree at the end of

https://code.google.com/p/stan/source/browse/rstan/rstan/R/stanfit-class.R

sflist2stanfit <- function(sflist) {
  # merge a list of stanfit objects into one
  # Args:
  #   sflist, a list of stanfit objects, each element of which
  #   should have equal length of `iter`, `warmup`, and `thin`.
  # Returns:
  #   A new stanfit objects have all the chains in each element of sf_list.
  #   The date would be where the new object is created.
  # Note:
  #   * method get_seed would not work well for this merged
  #     stanfit object. But all the information is still there.
  #   * When print function is called, the sampler is obtained
  #     only from the first chain.
  #
  sf_len <- length(sflist)
  if (sf_len < 2) stop("'sflist' should have more than 1 elements")
  if (!is.list(sflist) ||
      any(sapply(sflist, function(x) !is(x, "stanfit")))) {
    stop("'sflist' must be a list of 'stanfit' objects")
  }
  if (any(sapply(sflist, function(x) x@mode != 0))) {
    stop("each 'stanfit' object in 'sflist' must contain samples")
  }
  for (i in 2:sf_len) {
    if (!identical(sflist[[i]]@sim$pars_oi, sflist[[1]]@sim$pars_oi) ||
        !identical(sflist[[i]]@sim$dims_oi, sflist[[1]]@sim$dims_oi))
      stop("parameters in element ", i, " (stanfit object) is different from in element 1")
    if (sflist[[i]]@sim$n_save[1] != sflist[[1]]@sim$n_save[1] ||
        sflist[[i]]@sim$warmup2[1] != sflist[[1]]@sim$warmup2[1])
      stop("all 'stanfit' objects should have equal length of iterations and warmup")
  }
  n_chains = sum(sapply(sflist, function(x) x@sim$chains))
  sim = list(samples = do.call(c, lapply(sflist, function(x) x@sim$samples)),
             chains = n_chains,
             iter = sflist[[1]]@sim$iter,
             thin = sflist[[1]]@sim$thin,
             warmup = sflist[[1]]@sim$warmup,
             n_save = rep(sflist[[1]]@sim$n_save[1], n_chains),
             warmup2 = rep(sflist[[1]]@sim$warmup2[1], n_chains),
             thin = rep(sflist[[1]]@sim$thin[1], n_chains),
             permutation = do.call(c, lapply(sflist, function(x) x@sim$permutation)),
             pars_oi = sflist[[1]]@sim$pars_oi,
             dims_oi = sflist[[1]]@sim$dims_oi,
             fnames_oi = sflist[[1]]@sim$fnames_oi,
             n_flatnames = sflist[[1]]@sim$n_flatnames)
  nfit <- new("stanfit",
              model_name = sflist[[1]]@model_name,
              model_pars = sflist[[1]]@model_pars,
              par_dims  = sflist[[1]]@par_dims,
              mode = 0L,
              sim = sim,
              inits = do.call(c, lapply(sflist, function(x) x@inits)),
              stan_args = do.call(c, lapply(sflist, function(x) x@stan_args)),
              stanmodel = sflist[[1]]@stanmodel,
              date = date(),
              .MISC = new.env())
  invisible(nfit)
}

Optimal in what sense?  It's very easy to change.

I should explain what we're doing more clearly in
the manual.  I plugged in the L'Ecuyer RNG with
a seed for chain 1.  Then each subsequent chain
uses skip-ahead so the random numbers don't clash.
I used a very very large skip ahead that would
require a whole lot of random numbers per chain.
I'll look it up and put the right numbers in.

The period of L'Ecuyer is pretty good, but
speed isn't optimal.  And if you do things like
use consecutive or close seeds, you get closely
related random numbers at least initially.

The C++ code lets you plug and play Boost RNGs
(or other RNGs implementing their concept.)

- Bob

I think what Ben was trying to say it is *not* possible to pass chain_id to stan().  Whatever you give as chain_id for stan() (as it has ... argument, so it would not complain), the real chain ids would be from 1 to the number of chains (parameter chains). So I should let stan() honor user supplied chain_id in rstan 1.0.3.  Then the best way would be to let all stan call have the same seed, but different chain_id's.

Ah. I thought stan() would pass everything in its ... to Stan, but maybe not until 1.0.3. In any event, supplying the chain_id does not hurt now, and it may do something good in a future version of rstan / Stan.

> So it is important to have very different seeds for stan if run in parallel in rstan 1.0.2.

As it stands right now, using mclapply() is not so bad because stan() by default passes a pseudo-random seed from R to Stan because

seed = sample.int(.Machine$integer.max, 1)

by default. Those $chains values are realized sequentially in the main R process before it gets forked $chains times and starts $chains Stan processes. That is not the best thing in the world, but if you are only doing a few chains for a few thousand iterations then it probably won't compromise the independence of the chains too badly.

If you were using another parallelizing function (such as on Windows) that does not fork the main R process but actually starts $chains new R processes in the background at approximately the same time, then sample.int <http://sample.int>() could produce the same or similar seeds. I was hoping that specifying chain_id would help, but I guess rstan 1.0.2 doesn't pass that to Stan.

> So I should let stan() honor user supplied chain_id in rstan 1.0.3.  Then the best way would be to let all stan call have the same seed, but different chain_id's.

That would be good. Particularly if we upgrade from the Boost PRNG we are using now.

I would be worried about typos. Matt could probably come up with an example where it makes things worse, but in general it should be an option for any distribution in the location-scale family

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Location-scale_family

I think the Matt trick is primarily intended for parameters in multilevel models in order to reduce the correlations in the posterior distribution of the parameters. Doing it when data on are the left-hand side of the ~ probably shouldn't affect things much.

Ben

For us Windows folks, it doesn't look like the parallel package works.  Here is my attempt using snow.

# compile model
fit.stan <- stan(model_code = m2.SEM, data = bdat, iter = 1, chains = 1, verbose = T)

# load snow
library(snow)
# setup cluster with two cores
cl <- makeCluster(c("localhost","localhost"), type = "SOCK")

# create list with data, parameters to be traced, compiled model, and function for generating initial values
cldata <- list(data=bdat, params=params, fit = fit.stan, inits=its)
clusterEvalQ(cl, library(rstan))    # loads rjags library on each node
clusterExport(cl, "cldata")         # loads cldata on each node

stanmod <- function(i) {
                        stan(fit = cldata$fit, data = cldata$data, inits = cldata$inits(),
                                  iter = 700, warmup = 250, thin = 2, chains = 1,
                                  pars = cldata$params)
}
stan.out <- clusterApply(cl, 1:2, stanmod)
stopCluster(cl)

Obviously, this function can be cleaned up to supply the iter, warmup, and thin values directly to stanmod.

More importantly, you probably want to follow the sflist2stanfit approach and pull out the samples for post-processing using stan.out[[1]]@sim$samples or something like as.mcmc.list(lapply(stan.out, function(x){as.mcmc(extract(x, inc_warmup = F)[,1,])})).

Hope this isn't too daft!
Andrew

Hi all,

I'm just starting to play with Stan and building up to a multi-level IRT model.  My data are all Likert-scale, so I'm starting by extending these examples to work like a GRM rather than an IRT.  From my reading of the documentation, it looks like making these models work with ordinal data is just a matter of switching bernoulli_logit to ordered_logistic, and adding a vector for cutpoints to the parameters (and to the ordered_logistic call).  Am I missing anything there?

Second, I've been reading the discussion of optimizing for speed, and wonder whether the sample code here can be vectorized more.  In the sample, you have

for (n in 1:N)
  y[n] ~ ordered_logistic( exp(log_gamma[q[n]]) * (alpha[jj[n]] - beta[kk[n]] + delta) , c);

One would like to eliminate the loop and have only:

y ~ ordered_logistic( foo , c)

Could you, then, write:

for (n in 1:N)
  foo[n] = exp(log_gamma[q[n]]) * (alpha[jj[n]] - beta[kk[n]] + delta);
y ~ ordered_logistic( foo , c)

And would this have any measurable effect on speed?

Or would it be better to create 3 local vectors (unrolling log_gamma, alpha, and beta), and then have:

y ~ ordered_logistic( exp(log_gamma_local * (alpha_local - beta_local) , c)

I guess I could just try it and see, but if this has already been hashed out, I'm happy to stand on the shoulders of giants.

Huh, it turns out that just substituting ordered_logistic (with Likert data) for bernoulli_logit (for properly bernoullified data) in the IRT sample makes it run slightly faster.

Looks like ordered_logistic doesn't have a vectorized form, so I couldn't test the vectorized alternatives with that, but I did try it with the bernoulli_logit function.

Just moving bernoulli_logit out of the loop using foo to hold the calculated vector did give a speed boost, but not nearly the boost that came from this (all other parts of the original file are unchanged:

model {
  row_vector[N] log_gamma_local;
  row_vector[N] alpha_local;
  row_vector[N] beta_local;

  alpha ~ normal(0,sigma_alpha);
  beta ~ normal(0,sigma_beta);
  log_gamma ~ normal(0,sigma_gamma);
  delta ~ cauchy(0,5);
  sigma_alpha ~ cauchy(0,5);
  sigma_beta ~ cauchy(0,5);
  sigma_gamma ~ cauchy(0,5);
  for (n in 1:N) {
    log_gamma_local[n] <- log_gamma[kk[n]];
    alpha_local[n] <- alpha[jj[n]];
    beta_local[n] <- beta[kk[n]];
  }
  y ~ bernoulli_logit(exp( dot_product(log_gamma_local , (alpha_local - beta_local +delta))));
}

This version seems to run about 3 times faster.

On Friday, October 12, 2012 4:09:08 PM UTC-4, Josh Rosenau wrote:
> Looks like ordered_logistic doesn't have a vectorized form, so I couldn't test the vectorized alternatives with that, but I did try it with the bernoulli_logit function.
>
> Just moving bernoulli_logit out of the loop using foo to hold the calculated vector did give a speed boost

Yes, loops involving assignment statements ( <- ) only are cheap. Loops involving sampling statements ( ~ or lp__ <- lp__ + whatever; ) are expensive because they change the log-posterior. So, if you are able to use a vectorized distribution, it is often worthwhile to take the sampling statement out of the loop even if you have to do a loop with assignment statements to line up the parameters.

Although Stan currently does not have an ordered_probit function, you might be able to recast your model like you would under a Gibbs sampler with data augmentation of a latent variable governed by the cutpoints. That would be a lot of effort to code (and might not work well), but in the end you would be able to vectorize the y_star ~ normal(mu, 1).

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Thanks to the help in this thread, as well as the speed tweaks
suggested in the "How can I speed up my code?" FAQ post, I think the
attached is a fast and sufficient solution to the hierarchical mixture
I'm seeking to model. While it will be improved when a VonMises is
eventually implemented, in the meantime I simply constrain the
variance of a Gaussian to let most of the mass fall within the data
bounds; certainly I expect the data to conform to this restriction. I
also avoided problems with the location of the Gaussian approaching
the bounds by first transforming (before modelling) the data to fall
within 0 to 1 (instead of -pi to pi), then modelling the location on
the logit scale. I haven't done extensive validation, but it seems to
fit the few simulated data sets I've thrown at it pretty quickly and
accurately.

I do have a couple (final?) questions though:

1) What are the priors implied by this specification? I *think* the
priors for mu1, mu2 and mu3 are uniform in the range permitted for
each, and similarly the priors for the correlation matrix is uniform
between -1 and 1 for each correlation, correct? While I actually don't
really have any more informative priors in my head for my data, I do
wonder what I should do in the future if I wanted non-uniform priors
implemented.

2) Is there a way to restrict the saved parameter samples to just a
subset of all parameters? There's 199 parameters in the full model,
but where I'm only really interested in 6 of them (mu1, mu2, mu3,
Tau.1.2, Tau.1.3., Tau.2.3.), it seems like it might be a waste of
memory to save all 199. Maybe I'm overestimating the memory costs or
possibly the utility of some of the other 193 parameters?

messages.body_plain:
On Friday, October 12, 2012 9:24:45 PM UTC-4, Mike Lawrence wrote:
> I do have a couple (final?) questions though:
>
> 1) What are the priors implied by this specification? I *think* the
> priors for mu1, mu2 and mu3 are uniform in the range permitted for
> each,

The default prior is always uniform over the support of the parameter.

> and similarly the priors for the correlation matrix is uniform
> between -1 and 1 for each correlation, correct?

This is a subtle but important misstatement: That prior for the correlation matrix is jointly uniform over KxK correlation matrices (symmetric, PSD, unit diagonal). If the prior were marginally uniform on [-1,1] for each of the K choose 2 correlations, then there would be a (large) region of the parameter space where the correlation matrix was not PSD. A mostly irrelevant fact is that under a jointly uniform prior, the marginal correlations are all scale-and-shifts of a symmetric beta distribution to the [-1,1] interval.

> While I actually don't really have any more informative priors in my head for my data, I do
> wonder what I should do in the future if I wanted non-uniform priors implemented.

At the moment, Stan doesn't have many great options for priors on a univariate parameter with bounded support on both sides. We should probably have a generalization of the beta distribution for these situations with a minimum, maximum, mean, and dispersion.

Stan supports an informative prior over a correlation matrix with the lkj_corr(eta) distribution. If eta == 1.0, the distribution is jointly uniform, so it is a (big) waste of time and RAM to call it. But you can choose eta to be something other than 1.0; in particular to the extent that eta is greater than 1.0, the lkj prior has a sharper mode at the identity matrix.

> 2) Is there a way to restrict the saved parameter samples to just a
> subset of all parameters? There's 199 parameters in the full model,
> but where I'm only really interested in 6 of them (mu1, mu2, mu3,
> Tau.1.2, Tau.1.3., Tau.2.3.), it seems like it might be a waste of
> memory to save all 199. Maybe I'm overestimating the memory costs or
> possibly the utility of some of the other 193 parameters?

Yes, instead of defining the nuisance parameters in the transformed parameters {} block, define them at the top of the model {} block.

Ben

On Sunday, October 14, 2012 4:29:09 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> thank you very much. When I tried your code, it first did not compile for me since stan complained about the 0-1 limitation for p in the model block. Are limitations not allowed there? Removing the upper and lower statements solved the problem and the model seems to work fine.

Sorry about that. Restrictions on the support of a local variable are not allowed (and are not checked) in the model {} block. But since the variable is on the (0,1) interval by construction, it is fine to remove the lower and upper bounds. I believe that transformations in the transformed parameters block are checked, so it is good to provide the bounds in that case.

> However, I tried to get rid of the p variable altogether and wrote
>
> for(i in 1:N) y[i] ~ binomial(Nmax, inv_logit(alpha + beta[Cs[i]] * time[i]) );
>
> in my model. This again produces the error that some chains do not converge at all and I see again the
>
> Warning (non-fatal rejection): Error in function stan::prob::cauchy_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Random variable is nan:0, but must not be nan!
>
> statement for one of the chains. This looks to me like bug - either in stan, the compiler or wherever; if you agree, I can provide more info.

When I do it with a large number of chains and a large number of iterations, sometimes it goes perfectly and sometimes one chain experiences a nan and never recovers. Many functions in Stan are not numerically stable, so things like this happen with some probability.

> Some more questions in this context:
>
> - Concerning the inv_logit transform: To me it is simply a transform of a given parameter, so why shouldn't I put it in the transformed parameter block? Should I always put inverse links into the model block? And if yes, which transformations should I then included in transformed parameters and which in the model?

The question is really: Do you want to analyze its posterior distribution? If yes, put it into the transformed parameters {} block. If no, put it in the model {} block. I assumed no since your R code did not reference those probabilities, but whichever choice you make "should" have no effect on the sampling, in theory. But in practice, maybe numeric instability issues are handled more gracefully when the probability is in the transformed parameters {} block because if it violates its bounds, then a non-fatal exception is thrown before the log-posterior is evaluated.

> - should I always limit my scale parameters by 0 and some upper bound, lets say 100 in the declarations or is a cauchy prior preferable?

In principle, it is a question of what you believe about the data-generating process. Andrew's paper recommended either of those, and maybe bounding on both sides is more numerically stable. What Andrew found to be objectionable in theory and problematic in practice were (nearly) improper priors over the entire positive half of the real line.

Ben

On 10/14/12 12:39 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Sunday, October 14, 2012 4:29:09 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
>
>     thank you very much. When I tried your code, it first did not compile for me since stan complained about the 0-1
>     limitation for p in the model block. Are limitations not allowed there? Removing the upper and lower statements
>     solved the problem and the model seems to work fine.
>
>
> Sorry about that. Restrictions on the support of a local variable are not allowed (and are not checked) in the model {}
> block. But since the variable is on the (0,1) interval by construction, it is fine to remove the lower and upper bounds.
> I believe that transformations in the transformed parameters block are checked, so it is good to provide the bounds in
> that case.

Yes, anywhere you can declare constraints, the
constraints are enforced at the end of the block
in which the variable is declared.

> When I do it with a large number of chains and a large number of iterations, sometimes it goes perfectly and sometimes
> one chain experiences a nan and never recovers. Many functions in Stan are not numerically stable, so things like this
> happen with some probability.

There are also basic functions, like 0.0 / 0.0 that
produce NaN.  In some cases, we can get around that.

If there are known places where you think we're doing
something at boundaries that we could make better
behaved than returning NaN or throwing an exception, let
us know and we can fix it.

>     Some more questions in this context:
>
>     - Concerning the inv_logit transform: To me it is simply a transform of a given parameter, so why shouldn't I put it
>     in the transformed parameter block? Should I always put inverse links into the model block? And if yes, which
>     transformations should I then included in transformed parameters and which in the model?
>
>
> The question is really: Do you want to analyze its posterior distribution? If yes, put it into the transformed
> parameters {} block. If no, put it in the model {} block. I assumed no since your R code did not reference those
> probabilities, but whichever choice you make "should" have no effect on the sampling, in theory.

We can work out the behavior based on the definitions
of the error checking in the manual.

Transformed parameters: constraints enforced at the end
of the model block

Parameters to probability functions: domain constraints
enforced when called

Given this behavior, if you have a variable that has to
be between 0 and 1, say because it's the parameter for a Bernoulli,
then declaring a constraint on the transformed parameter
catches the error before any of the model is executed.  Defining
it as a local variable in the model block will lead to the error
being caught the first time it's used.

All else being equal, trapping errors early is a good thing.

 > But in practice, maybe
> numeric instability issues are handled more gracefully when the probability is in the transformed parameters {} block
> because if it violates its bounds, then a non-fatal exception is thrown before the log-posterior is evaluated.

Please let us know if you run into reproducible numerical
stability issues.  We could definitely use better limiting
behavior in many cases.

In some cases, it's just plain old IEEE floating-point
arithmetic, like if you divde 0.0 / 0.0 somewhere.

>     - should I always limit my scale parameters by 0 and some upper bound, lets say 100 in the declarations or is a
>     cauchy prior preferable?
>
>
> In principle, it is a question of what you believe about the data-generating process. Andrew's paper recommended either
> of those, and maybe bounding on both sides is more numerically stable. What Andrew found to be objectionable in theory
> and problematic in practice were (nearly) improper priors over the entire positive half of the real line.

You can try both and see what effect they have on the posterior.
They will also have different posterior geometries (that is, the
covariance structure across the parameter values), which can make
one or the other more efficient in terms of drawing effective
samples.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 10/14/12 4:29 AM, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> Hi Ben,
>
> thank you very much. When I tried your code, it first did not compile for me since stan complained about the 0-1 limitation for p in the model block. Are limitations not allowed there? Removing the upper and lower statements solved the problem and the model seems to work fine. However, I tried to get rid of the p variable altogether and wrote
>
> for(i in 1:N) y[i] ~ binomial(Nmax, inv_logit(alpha + beta[Cs[i]] * time[i]) );
>
> in my model. This again produces the error that some chains do not converge at all and I see again the
>
> Warning (non-fatal rejection): Error in function stan::prob::cauchy_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Random variable is nan:0, but must not be nan!
>
> statement for one of the chains. This looks to me like bug - either in stan, the compiler or wherever; if you agree, I can provide more info.

No, it's not a bug per se, but it is a problem with
floating point arithmetic.

We should have a binomial_logit like we have a bernoulli_logit,
which is better behaved numerically because we can do some
algebra behind the scenes as the log probabilities are
calculated.

We really need to make this error message clearer.
It's confusing everyone.  Maybe something that says
it's not a bug.

The issue is not only the math library, but also the
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo simulations, which if they
aren't discretized at a fine enough grain can lead
to errors in the transforms.  But the problem isn't
always there, it's then when those parameters are used.

> Some more questions in this context:
>
> - Concerning the inv_logit transform: To me it is simply a transform of a given parameter, so why shouldn't I put it in the transformed parameter block? Should I always put inverse links into the model block? And if yes, which transformations should I then included in transformed parameters and which in the model?

You could put it there.  See my previous message.

In Stan, the decision should be made based on whether
you want the error checking in the transformed parameter
block and if you want printing.  It's too bad they're
linked together, because they're really independent
functions.

You don't need to do the BUGS thing, like this:

     for (n in 1:N) y_hat[n] <- alpha * x[n] + beta;
     for (n in 1:N) y[n] ~ normal(y_hat[n],sigma);

If you declare y_hat[n] as a transformed parameter,
you get n outputs, which you may not care about.  They'll
take space and time to write, but it might be negligible
compared to everything else going on depending on the model.

You can just write:

     for (n in 1:N) y[n] ~ normal(alpha * x[n] + beta, sigma);

or you can write:

     for (n in 1:N) {
       real y_hat;
       y_hat <- alpha * x[n] + beta;
       y[n] ~ normal(y_hat, sigma);
     }

These won't output the values.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] hierarchical mixture modelling
messages.body_plain:
On 10/12/12 9:24 PM, Mike Lawrence wrote:
> Thanks to the help in this thread, as well as the speed tweaks
> suggested in the "How can I speed up my code?" FAQ post, I think the
> attached is a fast and sufficient solution to the hierarchical mixture
> I'm seeking to model.

Great!

> While it will be improved when a VonMises is
> eventually implemented,

That's about to happen.  We have a new contributor
who's almost done with a nice vectorized version.

> ... in the meantime I simply constrain the

> variance of a Gaussian to let most of the mass fall within the data
> bounds; certainly I expect the data to conform to this restriction. I
> also avoided problems with the location of the Gaussian approaching
> the bounds by first transforming (before modelling) the data to fall
> within 0 to 1 (instead of -pi to pi), then modelling the location on
> the logit scale. I haven't done extensive validation, but it seems to
> fit the few simulated data sets I've thrown at it pretty quickly and
> accurately.

Isn't that a slightly different model?  (Not that
there's anything wrong with doing that.  Andrew
calls it "the Pinocchio Principle", because
"A model that is created solely for computational
reasons can take on a life of its own."
See Andrew's whole evolving statistical lexicon at:

http://andrewgelman.com/2009/05/handy_statistic/

> I do have a couple (final?) questions though:
>
> 1) What are the priors implied by this specification? I *think* the
> priors for mu1, mu2 and mu3 are uniform in the range permitted for
> each,

If priors aren't specified, that's what Stan assumes.  This
is proper for types such as lower-and-upper-bounded reals,
simplexes, and correlation matrices, and improper otherwise.

If you specify a prior, it in some sense multiplies by the
uniform to do the right thing (added on the log scale).

> and similarly the priors for the correlation matrix is uniform
> between -1 and 1 for each correlation, correct?

Ben already answered that in the negative -- it's uniform over
all positive definite covariance matrices (technically over
positive semi-definite -- the non positive definite subset
is very small in theory, but can occur in practice due to
numerical issues).

> While I actually don't
> really have any more informative priors in my head for my data, I do
> wonder what I should do in the future if I wanted non-uniform priors
> implemented.

You can use any old distribution with truncation.

The trick is keeping everything constrained properly.

> 2) Is there a way to restrict the saved parameter samples to just a
> subset of all parameters?

Not right now.  Stan saves all parameters, transformed
parameters, and generated quantities.  All random quantities
must be declared as one of these types.

In some cases, you can move transformed parameters into
local variables.

>  There's 199 parameters in the full model,
> but where I'm only really interested in 6 of them (mu1, mu2, mu3,
> Tau.1.2, Tau.1.3., Tau.2.3.), it seems like it might be a waste of
> memory to save all 199.

You're right -- that's mostly wasted memory to save them all
if you really don't need them.  (We're really bad in that we
save both sides of a symmetric covariance matrix.)

I would argue that you want to at least monitor all the
parameters for convergence and large enough effective sample
size, even if you don't want all of them.  I should call this
out in the manual somewhere.

 > Maybe I'm overestimating the memory costs or
> possibly the utility of some of the other 193 parameters?

It shouldn't be too bad in size unless you're storing
gazillions of them.  But it is mostly wasted, which is
a shame.

- Bob

messages.subject: location-scale "mat trick" for multivariate normal
messages.body_plain:
The FAQ for improving speed suggests to reduce correlations in posterior draws for higher-level hyperparameters under a multivariate Gaussian by drawing from from multi_normal() using a correlation matrix with location = 0 and then scaling and locating the result.   Suppose one has a matrix[T,D] delta where delta[t] ~ multi_normal(fred,S) for D x D covariance, S.   Would it be better  to draw a T x D matrix of standard normals, Z, and scale each row_vector, z[t], by the cholesky decomposition of S and then add mean, fred?   i suppose we avoid forming S under the suggested process, however, but such seems a small cost, given the correlation matrix and scale vector.  i know (from Ben) that even better is to directly update lp_ with the quadratic product kernel of the Gaussian.  maybe take the cholesky decomposition of the covariance matrix and compute the inverse of that in the absence of having gaussian elimination available.   i'd like to first get the simpler approach working, however.

--
Thank you, Terrance Savitsky

> My question is: why the estimated sigma values (3.136 and 3.192) are much larger than their assigned value (2.75)? Are there something wrong with my code?

I think your code is not wrong (although we would much prefer attachments than embedding everything in a post).

You can speed it up considerably by vectorizing the normals, as in

model {
    y1 ~ normal(alpha1, sigma1);
    y2 ~ normal(alpha2, sigma2);
}

Stan is not getting a great effective sample size on these standard deviation estimates, but they are close to what you would get from least squares, e.g. in R

On 10/16/12 3:32 PM, Shige Song wrote:
> Thanks for the help, Ben. Dropping the seed did lead to closer estimates of the sigma.

There's always a seed.  If you don't specify one, Stan
generates it randomly given the time.

> I did not expect setting random
> number seed can have such an effect.

It comes down to the initialization.  If you do
your own initial points, it won't matter nearly
as much for sampling.  But random inits, especially
with weak constraints, can lead to very bad initial
points that take a lot of time to adapt out of.

If you run long enough, adaptation should find a
better place and adapt to that before sampling.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: t-test
messages.body_plain:
On 10/16/12 4:45 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Tuesday, October 16, 2012 4:37:21 PM UTC-4, Shige wrote:
>
>     Can you be more specific about how to vectorize the model for this particular case? Thanks.
>
>
> The original model {} block was
>
> |
> model {
>        for (n in 1:n1)
>            y1[n] ~ normal(alpha1, sigma1);
>        for (n in 1:n2)
>            y2[n] ~ normal(alpha2, sigma2);
> }
> |
>
> This style is necessary for BUGS but involves n1 + n2 function calls.

The real issue is what those function calls (to normal_log(y1[n],alpha1,sigma1))
do.  Non-virtual function calls like this are pretty fast.

The problem is that every time you involve an expression
in the log probability calculation, you wind up allocating
memory for the expression in the expression tree stack,
calling its constructor (which can involve some copies by
reference) and then evaluating the virtual function call
for the chain rule during the gradient calculation.

What happens in the vectorized version is that one compound
expression gets put on the expression tree stack and
only one constructor is called and one virtual function for
the chain rule applied to the node during auto-dif.  There's
also less pointer chasing within the chain rule and more
locality because the vector data's stored contiguously as
double types.

On top of that, if all the arguments are not vectors,
some redundant calculations can be eliminated by some
algebra up front.

In Stan you can write it as
>
> |
> model {
>      y1 ~ normal(alpha1, sigma1);
>      y2 ~ normal(alpha2, sigma2);
> }
> |
>
> which is only two function calls and has several other optimizations.

See above :-)

- Bob

Dear Stan users,

I am experiencing rather weird numerical issues with Stan as very few chains go wild for my model. I put weakly informative priors on my parameters and let Stan initialize randomly the chains. However, when I start off many chains (12) for my model I regularly end up with one of the chains not converging at all in almost all the parameters. This single chain then leads to completely wrong results as it is totally off the scale of all the other parameters. My question now would be how to handle this situation? I could set initial values to MLE parameter estimates of a simpler model and let Stan refine them, but then each chain would start off with the same initial parameters which does not sound very well to me. So, what strategies apply in this case?

Moreover, is it possible to drop a chain from the stanfit object? If so, how can I identify the invalid chain and then get rid of it?

My model itself is a mixed effect logistic regression of longitudinal data taken from subjects under different treatments.

Thank you very much for your help.

Best,

However, when I start off many chains (12) for my model I regularly end up with one of the chains not converging at all in almost all the parameters. I could set initial values to MLE parameter estimates of a simpler model and let Stan refine them, but then each chain would start off with the same initial parameters which does not sound very well to me. So, what strategies apply in this case?
>
> Moreover, is it possible to drop a chain from the stanfit object? If so, how can I identify the invalid chain and then get rid of it?

We have seen situations like this, even for simple models, but haven't figured out the cause yet. I don't think there is a convenient way to drop a chain from a stanfit object. However, if you have the sflist2stanfit() function from the thread on parallel chains, you can avoid including a problematic chain in a stanfit object. Just call stan() 12 times (in serial or in parallel) with chains = 1, mark the good chains, and then assemble a stanfit object, like

chains <- mclapply(...)
good <- c(1:2,4,5:9,11:12)
posterior <- sflist2stanfit(chains[good])

Ben

> alpha[ subject-range category 2 ] ~ normal(mu_alpha[2], sigma_alpha[2])
>
> and so on. I saw that Eigen has support for vector.segment, so this kind of array indexing should be possible.

It is one thing to say that Eigen or C++ supports something and another thing to get the Stan parser to produce the corresponding C++ code. I guess you could use the Stan parser to generate a .cpp file and then manually edit the .cpp file to change those two lines to be more efficient. Note that your parameters may be std::vectors rather than Eigen objects, but you could hack in whatever iterators are valid for a std::vector. If you come up with something really good, let us know and Bob might be able to implement it in the parser.

> BTW, has someone tried to get Eigens support for the Intel MKL running with Stan?

Several months ago, I once verified that our tests work with the Intel MKL compiler. I didn't really test if code runs faster, but it certainly takes longer for the Intel MKL compiler to compile Stan code, which has lots of templates and metaprogramming. I don't think I defined whatever it is that makes Eigen use Intel MKL but it would probably work. The thing is that you would have to define that before compiling the whole Stan library, in addition to the specific model you are trying to estimate.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] numerical instability
messages.body_plain:
I have more notes below, but this may very well be
related to the patch Matt just made for initial adaptation.

We should release a new version soon with a bunch of
these fixes.

More inline below on specific issues.

> On Wednesday, October 17, 2012 11:11:43 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
>
>
>     Maybe, I don't know. I had 12 chains running 1000 iterations with 500 warmup steps. All but one chain equilibrated
>     to their final values after 200 steps at most. The one chain which went off was very far from the rest for all
>     parameters. The chain had a tendency towards the main bulk, but it was still after 1000 steps completely off, I
>     think one would have to wait really long to fix this. Running the chain much longer becomes a bit inconvenient as
>     this already took 4 hours or so. It is very odd to see all but one chain converge.

This isn't odd when you think about what's going
on in the implementation (some hints below).

>      > On Wednesday, October 17, 2012 7:50:00 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
>      > Dear Stan users,
>      >
>      > I am experiencing rather weird numerical issues with Stan as very few chains go wild for my model. I put weakly
>     informative priors

Stronger priors may not help if it's an init issue.

 > on my parameters and let Stan initialize randomly the chains. However, when I start off many
>     chains (12) for my model I regularly end up with one of the chains not converging at all in almost all the
>     parameters. This single chain then leads to completely wrong results as it is totally off the scale of all the other
>     parameters. My question now would be how to handle this situation? I could set initial values to MLE parameter
>     estimates of a simpler model and let Stan refine them, but then each chain would start off with the same initial
>     parameters which does not sound very well to me. So, what strategies apply in this case?
>      >
>      > Moreover, is it possible to drop a chain from the stanfit object? If so, how can I identify the invalid chain and
>     then get rid of it?

I don't know about the R interface, but
the problem we have with this in general is that
just pruning chains affects the balance of
the algorithm.  For instance, if problems arise
from two different modes, it's not technically wrong
to keep them both (though Stan would almost never
jump between modes with a big drop in log probability
in between).  Also, if one chain is walking around in
a fat tail and another in a trunk, it can take a long
time (in theory and practice) for them to converge
so that R-hat looks OK.

On 10/17/12 11:26 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
 > Until we figure out what the problem is, this is all speculation.
 > But I don't think the starting values or the number of
 > iterations are particularly relevant. If 11 out of 12 chains work,
 > the 12th should be able to recover from whatever
 > problem afflicted it, but that isn't happening for some reason.

This would be nice in principle, but floating-point arithmetic
is a harsh mistress.  If an init causes issues like NaN or underflow
or overflow, it's essentially unrecoverable.

In the command-line code, we check if there are NaN values
produced and restart a chain with new random inits if there is.
But only during the first part of warmup.  We should probably
think harder about this.

If arithmetic issues arise after inits, it'll just lead to
Metropolis rejection of all the subsequent samples (that is,
repeats of the same sample from an output perspective).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: vectorizing multi-level hierarchical models
messages.body_plain:
Most of our compute time is spent in auto-dif
and the rest in expensive function eval (log,
exp, lgamma, etc.)

You'll find that every matrix/array access, etc.,
uses a + 1 to index from 1.  This is really inefficient
compared to using iterators, but the cost of the +1 is
a negligible cost in the overall Stan code, so eliminating
it won't lead to much of a speedup.

There are lots of other places where iteration can
be sped up, but I seriously doubt it'll lead to
any measurable improvements in speed.

- Bob

On 10/17/12 10:01 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Wednesday, October 17, 2012 8:26:08 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
>
>     I fit kinetic parameters of subjects which have different treatments assigned. Per treatment I have a (possibly)
>     varying number of subject such that I end up writing model code like this:
>
>         for(i in 1:S) {
>            alpha[i] ~ normal(mu_alpha[SC[i]], sigma_alpha[SC[i]]);
>            beta[i] ~ normal(mu_beta[SC[i]], sigma_beta[SC[i]]);
>         }
>
>     Here, S is the total number of subjects and SC is the subject to category/treatment mapping. As you can see, this is
>     brute force for-looping. So is it possible to specify ranges for vectors and make vectorized statements like this:
>
>     alpha[ subject-range category 1 ] ~ normal(mu_alpha[1], sigma_alpha[1])
>     alpha[ subject-range category 2 ] ~ normal(mu_alpha[2], sigma_alpha[2])
>
>     and so on. I saw that Eigen has support for vector.segment, so this kind of array indexing should be possible.
>
>
> It is one thing to say that Eigen or C++ supports something and another thing to get the Stan parser to produce the
> corresponding C++ code. I guess you could use the Stan parser to generate a .cpp file and then manually edit the .cpp
> file to change those two lines to be more efficient. Note that your parameters may be std::vectors rather than Eigen
> objects, but you could hack in whatever iterators are valid for a std::vector. If you come up with something really
> good, let us know and Bob might be able to implement it in the parser.
>
>     BTW, has someone tried to get Eigens support for the Intel MKL running with Stan?
>
>
> Several months ago, I once verified that our tests work with the Intel MKL compiler. I didn't really test if code runs
> faster, but it certainly takes longer for the Intel MKL compiler to compile Stan code, which has lots of templates and
> metaprogramming. I don't think I defined whatever it is that makes Eigen use Intel MKL but it would probably work. The
> thing is that you would have to define that before compiling the whole Stan library, in addition to the specific model
> you are trying to estimate.
>
> Ben
>

> --
>
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] numerical instability
messages.body_plain:
As Bob says, far away from the typical set you can get extreme gradients that cause the numerical integration to diverge and yield mostly rejections.

The same behavior could also be indicative of p(typical point -> point) << 1.  Because of detailed balance p(point -> typical point) will also be much less than one: once you have the misfortune of transitioning to that point it will take forever to transition back to the typical set.  The more chains you run, and the longer you run them, the more likely you are to hit one of these unlikely regions.  Note that, if we reject on NaNs and infinities, then the first behavior can also be thought of in these terms.

messages.body_plain:
Douglas Bates vas escriure el dia dl, 08 oct 2012:

> What tools are popular for the analysis and visualization of samples
> created by stan?  In particular, I would be interested in tools that use
> both lp__ and the parameter values.

Hi all,

Although this was posted several days ago, I would like to add that there
is a new package in R called "ggmcmc" that is intended to do precisely
that: visual inspection of convergence. Now it only shows the usual plots
(densities, traceplots, running means, comparisons of full chain and last
part, autocorrelations, crosscorrelations, histograms and even
caterpillarplots), but I am planning to extend it to show visually the
formal diagnostics.

To use it in stan:
install.packages("ggmcmc", dependencies=TRUE)

Assume that 'm' is the result of a call to stan(), with the default 4
chains, then:
-----8<---------------
library(ggmcmc)
s <- extract(m, inc_warmup=FALSE)
s <- mcmc.list(mcmc(s[,1,-4]), mcmc(s[,2,-4]), mcmc(s[,3,-4]), mcmc(s[,4,-4]))
S <- ggs(s)
-----8<---------------

And now 'S' is an object ready to be plotted using ggmcmc
(ggs_traceplot(S), ggs_running(S), ...)

Or simply the wrapper function "ggmcmc(S)".

If stan is used without 'rstan', and the samples have been stored in
s_1.csv and s_2.csv:
-----8<---------------
library(coda)
s1 <- read.table("s_1.csv", sep=",", header=TRUE)
s2 <- read.table("s_2.csv", sep=",", header=TRUE)
s.mcmc <- mcmc.list(mcmc(s1[,-c(1:3)]), mcmc(s2[,-c(1:3)]))
S <- ggs(s.mcmc)
-----8<---------------

I have written a detailed example on how to process Stan samples in ggmcmc:
http://blog.xavier-fim.net/2012/10/processing-stan-samples-with-ggmcmc

And there is a general introduction to ggmcmc:
http://xavier-fim.net/packages/ggmcmc/

Hope this helps,

--
-  Xavier  -

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] working with rstan output
messages.body_plain:
On 10/17/12 11:58 PM, Daniel Hocking wrote:

 > I am currently going through Marc Kery's book, "Introduction to WinBUGS for Ecologists"
 > and trying to translate all of
 > the WinBUGS code into stan (using rstan).

Fantastic.  I hope you can share it on a web site
or something -- we can certainly supply space and
distribution for models.

Also, if you have time, we'd love to hear about what
you found hard or easy to use, and what features you'd
like to see.  We learned a whole lot when we coded the
BUGS examples, but we weren't trying to do posterior
inference, just ensure we got the same results as JAGS
did.

 > It's my way of learning stan so the current code might not be the most
 > efficient (e.g. I'm starting out with BUGS-like loops instead of vectorized functions).

Starting with code that works and then making it
more efficient is MUCH easier than the other way
around.

Vectorizing is pretty easy to do after the fact, too.

 > My primary question is how best
 > to use the posterior samples to calculate Bayesian p-values, posterior predictive distributions, and various goodness of
 > fit metrics.

You can calculate posterior inferences based on
parameters and data in the generated quantities block
from within Stan or you can calculate in R with
the results.  RStan is set up just like R2WinBUGS
and R2jags, so examples of posterior analysis using
those packages will transfer directly to RStan.

The advantage of doing it within Stan is that you can
define new random variables based on parameters and
treat them like their natural types.  If you do the
work back in R, you have to iterate over the vector
yourself (though R makes that pretty easy in many cases).

You can define new variables in the generated quantities
block the way you'd define deterministic nodes in BUGS.
But if you need them in the model, they have to be
transformed parameters.  Both generated quantities and
transformed parameters get printed.

(The reason to use generated quantities instead of transformed
parameters is that it's much more efficient -- the values are double
data types instead of auto-dif for gradients
at that point and we only compute generated quantities once per
iteration, not once per leapfrog step.  It's also clearer about
what's part of the model and what's posterior/transform analysis.)

 > For example, in Chapter 8 there is a simple linear regression assuming normality. The R and WinBUGS (using R2WinBUGS)
 > code is attached including data generation. In the model statement below, you can see that he generates new data and
 > calculates some derived parameters within the WinBUGS code.
 > |
 >
 > ### 8.4.1. Fitting the model
 > # Write model
 > sink("linreg.txt")
 > cat("
 > model {
 >
 >      # Priors
 >      alpha ~ dnorm(0,0.001)
 >      beta ~ dnorm(0,0.001)
 >      sigma ~ dunif(0, 100)
 >
 >      # Likelihood
 >      for (i in 1:n) {
 >      y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], tau)
 >      mu[i] <- alpha + beta*x[i]
 >      }
 >
 >      # Derived quantities
 >      tau <- 1/ (sigma * sigma)
 >      p.decline <- 1-step(beta)        # Probability of decline
 >
 >      # Assess model fit using a sums-of-squares-type discrepancy
 >      for (i in 1:n) {
 >      residual[i] <- y[i]-mu[i]        # Residuals for observed data
 >      predicted[i] <- mu[i]        # Predicted values
 >      sq[i] <- pow(residual[i], 2)    # Squared residuals for observed data
 >
 >      # Generate replicate data and compute fit stats for them
 >      y.new <http://y.new>[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], tau) # one new data set at each MCMC iteration
 >      sq.new <http://sq.new>[i] <- pow(y.new <http://y.new>[i]-predicted[i], 2)    # Squared residuals for new data
 >      }
 >      fit <- sum(sq[])            # Sum of squared residuals for actual data set
 >      fit.new <http://fit.new> <- sum(sq.new <http://sq.new>[])        # Sum of squared residuals for new data set
 >      test <- step(fit.new <http://fit.new> - fit)        # Test whether new data set more extreme
 >      bpvalue <- mean(test)            # Bayesian p-value
 > }
 >      ",fill=TRUE)
 > sink()
 > |

The derived quantities that are not used in the model
should go in derived quantities block.  But for transforms
of parameters like tau (precision), you need to use
a transformed parameter in Stan.  Of course, in Stan,
you don't need the precision, so it could be moved out
anyway if you even care about it.

 > He then uses these new data to calculate and plot various assessments of model fit as such:
 >
 > |
 >
 > ### 8.4.2. Goodness-of-Fit assessment in Bayesian analyses
 > plot(out$mean$predicted, out$mean$residual, main = "Residuals vs. predicted values",
 >       las = 1, xlab = "Predicted values", ylab = "Residuals")
 > abline(h = 0)
 >
 > lim <- c(0, 3200)
 > plot(out$sims.list$fit, out$sims.list$fit.new <http://fit.new>, main = "Graphical posterior predictive check",
 >       las = 1, xlab = "SSQ for actual data set", ylab = "SSQ for ideal (new) data sets", xlim = lim, ylim = lim)
 > abline(0, 1)
 >
 > mean(out$sims.list$fit.new <http://fit.new> > out$sims.list$fit)    # Bayesian p-value
 >
 >
 > ### 8.4.3. Forming predictions
 > predictions <- array(dim = c(length(x), length(out$sims.list$alpha)))
 > for(i in 1:length(x)){
 >    predictions[i,] <- out$sims.list$alpha + out$sims.list$beta*i
 > }
 > LPB <- apply(predictions, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025) # Lower bound
 > UPB <- apply(predictions, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975) # Upper bound

Anything collective like LPB and UPB need to be calculated
back in R because everything in Stan works on a draw-by-draw
basis.

For instance, even posterior means need to be calculated back in R.

So I guess the basic rule is:

   -- If it's a draw-by-draw operation on parameters/data, calculate
      in generated quantities

   -- If it's an operation over the entire sample of many draws,
      it has to be done back in R

 > I am wondering the best way to calculate these same parameters and how to derive the new data using rstan? I have the
 > following rstan code that runs the model but I am not sure how to best generate the new data and extract the parameter
 > estimates from the stan model fit to calculate the fit metrics. I'm not sure how much would be easier to do within stan
 > (generated quantities) or back in R (I am functionally literate in R and illiterate in C++).

You shouldn't need C++ for this.

 > Any suggestions would be
 > appreciated. I hope this question is not too vague and that I didn't dump too much code in this post.

More code is better than less.  As long as it's set off,
it's easy to skim.  If it's not there, I just wind up
guessing.

- Bob

No, I referred to the function call of stan in the rstan package:

init
One of digit 0, string "0" or "random", a function that returns a list, or a list of initial parameter values with which to indicate how the initial values of parameters are specified. "0": initialize all to be zero on the unconstrained support; "random": randomly generated; list: a list of lists equal in length to the number of chains (parameter chains), where each list in the list of lists specifies the initial values of parameters by name for the corresponding chain. function: a function that returns a list for specifying the initial values of parameters for a chain. The function can take an optional parameter chain_id.

Just type in ?stan in R.

Best,

Sebastian

messages.body_plain:
I got the following error when running the 8 school examples on a MacBook:

posterior <- sflist2stanfit(posterior) # see below for function definition

Error in FUN(X[[1L]], ...) :
  no slot of name "mode" for this object of class "stanfit"

Song

On Friday, October 12, 2012 12:14:45 AM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:

> Good news everyone (particularly people who are willing to help us test)! Jiqiang wrote a function that will be included in rstan 1.0.3 that facilitates running chains in parallel. In particular, you can do something like
>

> stopifnot(require(rstan))
>
> schools_dat <- list(J = 8,
>                     y = c(28,  8, -3,  7, -1,  1, 18, 12),
>                     sigma = c(15, 10, 16, 11,  9, 11, 10, 18))
>
> eight_schools <- stan(file = "http://wiki.stan.googlecode.com/git/rstangettingstarted/8schools.stan",
>                       data = schools_dat, iter = 1, chains = 1) # just get it to compile the model
>
> library(

> parallel) # or some other parallelizing package
> chains <- 8
>
> posterior <- mclapply(1:chains, mc.cores = chains, FUN = function(chain) { # or another parallelizing function
>                stan(fit = eight_schools, data = schools_dat, chains = 1, verbose = FALSE, refresh = -1, chain_id=chain)
>              })
>
> posterior <- sflist2stanfit(posterior) # see below for function definition
> print(posterior)
> plot(posterior)

>
> where the necessary new function sflist2stanfit() is defined at the end of this post and is also attached.
>
> Some things to note. In the example above, I first ran the eight schools model for one iteration of one chain just to get the code to compile. Then I passed that eight_schools object to the fit argument of stan() in each of the eight chains (with the defaults for warmup, iter, etc.). This route avoids having to recompile the code eight times and will work for mclapply() in the parallel package, which executes the function locally on a multicore machine. Note that mclapply() does not do anything in parallel on Windows, so you need to use an alternative parallelizing library / function in that case.
>
> This route will probably not work if you are using the snow package or a similar package to execute the chains on a remote server because the remote server will not know what to do with the code compiled on your laptop. In that case, you would need to specify file or model_code rather than fit, so that the remote server would compile the code for each chain. Also, if file is a filepath on your laptop, the remote server will not be able to access it, so you would need to upload your .stan file to a readable directory on the remote server and specify file accordingly. Similarly, the data somehow need to be available on the remote server and the remote server obviously needs to have rstan installed and loaded. Note that stanfit objects can be quite large in size, so you could be pulling GB of uncompressed data from the remote server to your laptop at the end.
>
> If you have access to some sort of computer lab with a bunch of physical PCs that have rstan but are not networked, you could execute stan() with chains = 1 on each PC, save the  resulting stanfit object to a USB stick with something like save(chain_3, file = "chain_3.RData", compress = "xz"), use the load() command to load each .RData object onto a common machine, put them into a list, and use sflist2stanfit() to consolidate them into a stanfit object that can be analyzed by the tools in the rstan package. Note that each chain needs to be given a different object name to avoid them overwriting each other when you load() them onto the common machine.
>
> For the high-performance (including parallel) capabilities that are available in R or R packages, execute help(package = parallel) in R or see
>
> http://cran.r-project.org/web/views/HighPerformanceComputing.html
>
> Ben (but mostly Jiqiang)
>
> P.S. The new function below can be pasted in now but is now defined in the rstan tree at the end of
>
> https://code.google.com/p/stan/source/browse/rstan/rstan/R/stanfit-class.R
>
> sflist2stanfit <- function(sflist) {
>   # merge a list of stanfit objects into one
>   # Args:
>   #   sflist, a list of stanfit objects, each element of which
>   #   should have equal length of `iter`, `warmup`, and `thin`.
>   # Returns:
>   #   A new stanfit objects have all the chains in each element of sf_list.
>   #   The date would be where the new object is created.
>   # Note:
>   #   * method get_seed would not work well for this merged
>   #     stanfit object. But all the information is still there.

messages.subject: Will STAN address these modelling and sampling limitations in WinBugs
messages.subject_clean: Will STAN address these modelling and sampling limitations in WinBugs
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am a WinBugs user that is very excited about using STAN based on what I have read in the manual. Before I jump in, I'm wondering if STAN can deal with two problems I have encountered in WinBugs due to limitations of its modelling environment:

1) 'multiple definitions of node'. This error occurs when I calculate a parameter as a function of data and other parameters as a logical expression, but also assume the parameter is part of a stochastic distribution (say the order of a binomial). I think this limitation is due to the DAG structure of WinBugs, and I'm hoping STAN eliminates this issue.

2) 'unable to choose update method'. According to WB documentation, this occurs if more than one binomial response is assumed to share the same order parameter. From the documentation, this has something to do with the sampler, and I'm hoping the substantially revised sampler in STAN will no longer have this limitation.

Will STAN get around these problems?

Any thoughts much appreciated,

Josh Korman

> Thank you Ben and Bob, the general discussion is very helpful. I will be happy to share my rstan code for Kery's WinBUGS examples, although they may be better in combination with Shige since I am still quite a novice in R as well as BUGS and Stan.
>
> I would also be happy to share my experiences to help you improve Stan and rstan for end users like myself.

Thanks. We'll probably adjust the manual along the lines of what you suggested.

> There seems to be sufficient information for running all the models I've tried but more information for post processing would be very helpful. The only other thing that I can think of that has been confusing is lp_. There is a little about it in the manual but more information would be useful.

It is just the value of the log-posterior evaluated at the realization of the parameters.

> Back to my example, I may have been generous when I claimed functional literacy in R because I am not sure I fully grasp your method of extracting and using the posterior samples
>
>
> y_rep <- apply(posterior, MARGIN = 1:2, FUN = function(draw) {
>   rnorm(n, mean = draw[grepl("^mu", names(draw))], sd = draw["sigma"])
> })
>
> I can understand what it does in the end but I can't figure it out enough to use it myself in other circumstances. For example, how would I go about creating a vector of the mean mu values if I wanted to make plots similar to Kery:

I can't actually make those plots because I don't have WinBUGS, but I can guess what they look like. Richard had a nice suggestion about using lists of arrays. In your case, I think a big array is fine, but you just need to know how to manipulate it.

If you wanted a vector of 16 values where the i-th element was mu[i] averaged over the 5000 iterations from each of 3 chains, I would do

mu_means <- apply(posterior[,,grepl("^mu",dimnames(posterior)[[3]])], 3, mean)

In your case, posterior is 5000 iterations by 3 chains by 69 parameters. So, grepl("^mu",dimnames(posterior)[[3]])] extracts the parameters whose first two letters are mu, leaving a 5000 by 3 by 16 array. The apply() command applies the specified function to the specified dimension of the resulting array, in this case the mean function to the third dimension. Thus, mu_means is

> as.matrix(mu_means)
           [,1]
mu[1]  41.98327
mu[2]  40.31490
mu[3]  38.64653
mu[4]  36.97816
mu[5]  35.30979
mu[6]  33.64142

On 10/18/12 12:42 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Thursday, October 18, 2012 12:18:33 PM UTC-4, Daniel Hocking wrote:

>     There seems to be sufficient information for running all the models I've tried but more information for post
>     processing would be very helpful. The only other thing that I can think of that has been confusing is lp_. There is
>     a little about it in the manual but more information would be useful.
>
>
> It is just the value of the log-posterior evaluated at the realization of the parameters.

In the output, lp__ is the accumulated total unnormalized
log probability.  By Bayes's rule, with theta params and
y data, we have

   p(theta|y)  oc  p(theta,y)  oc  exp(lp__)

At any given point in the program's execution, the value
of lp__ is the log probability accumulated up to that point
in the program's execution.  That's why you can add to it.

Writing

    y ~ normal(mu,sigma);

is really just syntactic sugar for

    lp__ <- lp__ + normal_log(y,mu,sigma);

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, October 18, 2012 12:22:11 PM UTC-4, Josh Korman wrote:
> I am a WinBugs user that is very excited about using STAN based on what I have read in the manual. Before I jump in, I'm wondering if STAN can deal with two problems I have encountered in WinBugs due to limitations of its modelling environment:

I haven't used WinBUGS much in a long time, so I am guessing. But I am guessing that these are not going to be a problem in Stan.

>  1) 'multiple definitions of node'. This error occurs when I calculate a parameter as a function of data and other parameters as a logical expression, but also assume the parameter is part of a stochastic distribution (say the order of a binomial). I think this limitation is due to the DAG structure of WinBugs, and I'm hoping STAN eliminates this issue.

Pretty sure this is not going to be a problem. See appendix C of the Stan manual. The code in the .stan file is parsed to a C++ file and works as would be expected. So, you can define a variable and then redefine it later, but you can't use it before it is defined and allocated. Stan doesn't do DAG structures; everything hinges on the textual representation of the model in the .stan file.

> 2) 'unable to choose update method'. According to WB documentation, this occurs if more than one binomial response is assumed to share the same order parameter. From the documentation, this has something to do with the sampler, and I'm hoping the substantially revised sampler in STAN will no longer have this limitation.

We only have 3 variations on the HMC sampler, but the default one is usually good enough because it is adaptive. You won't get an error message like this, but whether you will get a large number of effective samples from that posterior distribution remains to be seen.

It is hard to say anything for sure given the particularities of WinBUGS and your data. Just read the Stan manual and the FAQ thread, give Stan a try, and ask here if you have more questions.

Ben

> I am a WinBugs user that is very excited about using STAN based on what I have read in the manual. Before I jump in, I'm
> wondering if STAN can deal with two problems I have encountered in WinBugs due to limitations of its modelling environment:

> 1) 'multiple definitions of node'. This error occurs when I calculate a parameter as a function of data and other
> parameters as a logical expression, but also assume the parameter is part of a stochastic distribution (say the order of
> a binomial). I think this limitation is due to the DAG structure of WinBugs, and I'm hoping STAN eliminates this issue.

It would help if you gave us a concrete example of what
you want to do.

You can usually work around this problem indirectly in WinBUGS itself
by defining auxiliary nodes.

Stan does not permit assignments to parameters.

Transformed parameters may be assigned and reassigned.
Local variables can also be assigned and reassigned.
So it would be OK in Stan to do this:

   model {
     real sum;

     sum <- 0;
     for (n in 1:N) sum <- sum + x[n];
   }

Stan also lets you put anything on the left-hand side of
a sampling statement, but then it's up to you to add the
log Jacobian to lp__.

   model {
       sqrt(1/tau) ~ uniform(0,100);
       lp__ <- lp__ + log(

   }

> 2) 'unable to choose update method'. According to WB documentation, this occurs if more than one binomial response is
> assumed to share the same order parameter.

You won't get that error in Stan because we can
sample from anything that you can express in the
language.  WinBUGS has this problem in some cases
if one of its sampling strategies (see the manual
for the four or five that are used in different cases)
cannot be applied to the structure of the problem.

I'm again not sure what exactly you are trying to
do from this description.  An example would help.

Stan does not have discrete parameters.  So you
can't have n as a parameter in:

   n ~ binomial(N,theta);

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

Thanks for your reply.

I have included a simplified example that gets at my multiple definition
problem. Here I want to estimate abundance from two population (N[]) and
assume that each of these estimates comes from a hyper distribution with a
fixed value for tau. The objective is to estimate the overall abundance
(SuperN) as an information weighted average of the two estimates conditional
on the fixed value of tau. This works fine using the uncommented lines
(expu<- and u~dpois) below. Problem is that in my more complex model, N is a
function of other estimated parameters so need to do something like the two
commented-out lines, which won't work in WinBugs because N is defined twice
(as a logical expression and as a stochastic node).

As for as you second point, you say that STAN cannot estimate discrete
parameters. Would N from u~dbin(theta, N) be estimable if you allow N to be
continuous rather than discrete? Or is the order of a binomial (e.g. N in
this example) just not estimable in STAN?

Thanks,

Josh

Example CODE

r, M, and u are data, p,N, and superN are parameters to be estimated.

model
{
	mu~dnorm(0,1.0E-6)		#hyper prior on log of single
escapement estimate

	for (i in 1:2)
	{
		p[i]~dbeta(1,1)		#uninformative prior n p
		r[i]~dbin(p[i],M[i])	#binomial likelihood to estimate
capture probability p given recaps (r) and marks release (M)

		logN[i]~dnorm(mu,tau)	#log N for each population comes
from a common (super) distribution)
		N[i]<-exp(logN[i])		#transform

		#The following two lines work as expected
		expu[i]<-N[i]*p[i]	#expected number of unmarked fish
captured on 2nd pass given N and p
		u[i]~dpois(expu[i])	#This makes N[i] a stochastic node
which allows HBM to work

		#Replacing the previous 2 lines with the following 2 does
not work due to multiple definitions of node N[]
		#u[i]~dbin(p[i],N[i])
		#N[i]<-u[i]/p[i]

	}
	SuperN<-exp(mu)			#This is the single estimate based
on information across populations

}

> what I have read in the manual. Before I jump in, I'm wondering if STAN
can deal with two problems I have encountered in WinBugs due to limitations
