> a parameter as a function of data and other parameters as a logical
> expression, but also assume the parameter is part of a stochastic
distribution (say the order of a binomial). I think this limitation is due
to the DAG structure of WinBugs, and I'm hoping STAN eliminates this issue.

It would help if you gave us a concrete example of what you want to do.

You can usually work around this problem indirectly in WinBUGS itself by
defining auxiliary nodes.

Stan does not permit assignments to parameters.

Transformed parameters may be assigned and reassigned.
Local variables can also be assigned and reassigned.
So it would be OK in Stan to do this:

   model {
     real sum;

     sum <- 0;
     for (n in 1:N) sum <- sum + x[n];
   }

Stan also lets you put anything on the left-hand side of a sampling
statement, but then it's up to you to add the log Jacobian to lp__.

   model {
       sqrt(1/tau) ~ uniform(0,100);
       lp__ <- lp__ + log(
   }

> 2) 'unable to choose update method'. According to WB documentation,
> this occurs if more than one binomial response is assumed to share the
same order parameter.

You won't get that error in Stan because we can sample from anything that
you can express in the language.  WinBUGS has this problem in some cases if
one of its sampling strategies (see the manual for the four or five that are
used in different cases) cannot be applied to the structure of the problem.

I'm again not sure what exactly you are trying to do from this description.
An example would help.

Stan does not have discrete parameters.  So you can't have n as a parameter
in:

   n ~ binomial(N,theta);

- Bob

> I have included a simplified example that gets at my multiple definition
> problem. Here I want to estimate abundance from two population (N[]) and
> assume that each of these estimates comes from a hyper distribution with a
> fixed value for tau. The objective is to estimate the overall abundance
> (SuperN) as an information weighted average of the two estimates conditional
> on the fixed value of tau. This works fine using the uncommented lines
> (expu<- and u~dpois) below. Problem is that in my more complex model, N is a
> function of other estimated parameters so need to do something like the two
> commented-out lines, which won't work in WinBugs because N is defined twice
> (as a logical expression and as a stochastic node).
>
> As for as you second point, you say that STAN cannot estimate discrete
> parameters. Would N from u~dbin(theta, N) be estimable if you allow N to be
> continuous rather than discrete? Or is the order of a binomial (e.g. N in
> this example) just not estimable in STAN?

The function signatures for the distributions are in the
manual -- binomial(N,theta) requires N to be an integer.
(We're not using the R notation dbin() for pmfs and pdfs).

Unfortunately, the discretizing transforms like floor()
lose derivative information because they're flat step
functions.  So while we allow them as transforms, they don't
play into the log probability (we should make that clearer
in the manual).

Stan also uses different parameterizations than BUGS for
some distros (e.g., deviation rather than precision for
normals).

More below.

> Example CODE
>
> r, M, and u are data, p,N, and superN are parameters to be estimated.
>
> model
> {
> 	mu~dnorm(0,1.0E-6)		#hyper prior on log of single
> escapement estimate
>
> 	for (i in 1:2)
> 	{
> 		p[i]~dbeta(1,1)		#uninformative prior n p
> 		r[i]~dbin(p[i],M[i])	#binomial likelihood to estimate
> capture probability p given recaps (r) and marks release (M)
>
> 		logN[i]~dnorm(mu,tau)	#log N for each population comes
> from a common (super) distribution)
> 		N[i]<-exp(logN[i])		#transform
>
> 		#The following two lines work as expected
> 		expu[i]<-N[i]*p[i]	#expected number of unmarked fish
> captured on 2nd pass given N and p
> 		u[i]~dpois(expu[i])	#This makes N[i] a stochastic node
> which allows HBM to work
>
> 		#Replacing the previous 2 lines with the following 2 does
> not work due to multiple definitions of node N[]
> 		#u[i]~dbin(p[i],N[i])
> 		#N[i]<-u[i]/p[i]

I don't understand what you'd like this to do.

Stan is imperative, so what would happen in Stan is
that you'd define N[i] the second time and never use it.

If you just want to sample u[i] twice because its
probability is a product, that's OK in Stan:

    u[i] ~ poisson(exp(logN[i]) * p[i]);

    u[i] ~ binomial(floor(exp(logN[i])), p[i]);

That'll result in the following effect on the probability
function being defined:

   p(u,...) propto poisson(u[i]|...) * binomial(u[i]|...)

What's the log probability function supposed to be?

Then if you want to look at something, just define a new
generated quantity for it.

- Bob

function).

Josh

messages.body_plain:
The short answer is that discrete random
quantities don't play nicely with Hamiltonian
Monte Carlo.  Geometrically there's a discontinuity due
to the step() function, which is bad news.

In practice, Stan loses the connection between slope[j,i]
and the log probability because the step function flattens
it so the derivative is zero where it's defined.  You want
that binomial to have some effect on the slopes, I'd think.

I should talk about the dangers of step() in the manual.
I added yet another to-do item to that effect.

- Bob

> On 10/16/12 4:45 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> > On Tuesday, October 16, 2012 4:37:21 PM UTC-4, Shige wrote:
> >
> >     Can you be more specific about how to vectorize the model for this particular case? Thanks.
> >
> >
> > The original model {} block was
> >
> > |
> > model {
> >        for (n in 1:n1)
> >            y1[n] ~ normal(alpha1, sigma1);
> >        for (n in 1:n2)
> >            y2[n] ~ normal(alpha2, sigma2);
> > }
> > |
> >
> > This style is necessary for BUGS but involves n1 + n2 function calls.
>
> The real issue is what those function calls (to normal_log(y1[n],alpha1,sigma1))
> do.  Non-virtual function calls like this are pretty fast.
>
> The problem is that every time you involve an expression
> in the log probability calculation, you wind up allocating
> memory for the expression in the expression tree stack,
> calling its constructor (which can involve some copies by
> reference) and then evaluating the virtual function call
> for the chain rule during the gradient calculation.
>
> What happens in the vectorized version is that one compound
> expression gets put on the expression tree stack and
> only one constructor is called and one virtual function for
> the chain rule applied to the node during auto-dif.  There's
> also less pointer chasing within the chain rule and more
> locality because the vector data's stored contiguously as
> double types.
>
> On top of that, if all the arguments are not vectors,
> some redundant calculations can be eliminated by some
> algebra up front.
>
>
> In Stan you can write it as
> >
> > |
> > model {
> >      y1 ~ normal(alpha1, sigma1);
> >      y2 ~ normal(alpha2, sigma2);
> > }
> > |
> >
> > which is only two function calls and has several other optimizations.
>
> See above :-)

>
>
> - Bob

On Saturday, October 20, 2012 7:40:18 AM UTC-4, Shige wrote:
> I did some more experiments. This time, I increased the sample size from 60 and 40 to 60,000 and 40,000 to see how well Stan handles data of this size. It did not take long for the program to run but the results (out.txt) are quite surprising: the "n_eff" is 2 for five of the six coefficients. One would expect with 20,000 iterations and 10,000 warmup, the results should be rather  stable.
>
> By the way, I am running the most recent git version of rstan.

Here at Stan World Headquarters, we have actually been working with your example for a few days but with 600 and 400 observations. A few bugs in rstan have been fixed and we will probably release v1.0.3 next week. But the basic problem in your case is that by default, Stan starts with uniform draws of the parameters from the [-2,2] interval. In your case, the true means are 105 and 77.5, which is very far away. If you look at

> lp <- get_logposterior(fit, inc_warmup = TRUE)
> sapply(lp, head)
              [,1]           [,2]         [,3]          [,4]
[1,] -38854764.995 -201405126.509 -6473613.053 -41854200.654
[2,]     -5119.183      -5054.171    -5037.778     -6651.749
[3,]     -5039.239      -5053.858    -5036.749     -5030.744
[4,]     -5040.267      -5054.297    -5007.958     -5030.275
[5,]     -5038.682      -5054.230    -4998.652     -5030.858
[6,]     -5039.415      -5053.292    -3915.622     -5030.384

you can see that the first iteration is just awful for all four chains. The next few iterations are much, much better but still really, really bad compared to the truth which is around -1500.  And sometimes one or more of the chains never makes it to the mode. We hope to do better, but maybe not in the next (few) release(s).

In the meantime, you can either standardize the input or provide reasonable initial values. Both of those should work fine regardless of the number of observations.

Ben

1. this function would not work when permuted = FALSE, as in latter case, the returned object is not a list, but an array.

On Thursday, October 18, 2012 11:33:48 AM UTC-4, Richard McElreath wrote:
> I do a lot of simulating from the posterior, and what has simplified a lot of my R code for doing that is to convert the samples in the rstan object into a list of arrays. This is useful, because a matrix of varying effects samples could have dimension (200,9,10000), i.e. 200 clusters, 9 effects, and 10k samples. Simulating across these samples is inconvenient with rstan results, because the samples are stored in a "flat" format in which every parameter is a separate vector, not an element of an array. So it's hard to use apply or even merely loop over parameter indices. I got spoiled by mcarray output from rjags, perhaps.
>
> Here's the function I use to make rstan samples into a list of arrays:
>
> stripstan <- function( object , pars=NULL , permuted=TRUE , ... ) {
>     result <- list()
>     if ( is.null(pars) )
>         pseq <- 1:length(object@par_dims)
>     else
>         pseq <- pars
>     for ( i in pseq ) {
>         name <- names(object@par_dims)[i]
>         result[[ name ]] <- extract( object , name , permuted=permuted , ... )[[1]]
>     }
>     result
> }
>
> That will produce a list of arrays, so I can then use apply to marginalize or for to loop over parameters as needed, using vectorized code to apply calculations to all samples.
>
> This isn't a direct answer to your question, but it's a bit of infrastructure that has saved me a lot of awkward extract() fiddling.

That is what I meant. You can't specify a factor in the data{} section of a .stan file. You would need to convert the factor inside R to integer codes. So, if for example, you had a factor in R like

data(InsectSprays)

int_spray <- as.integer(InsectSprays$spray)

messages.body_plain:
Parsing and terminology issues inline below.

On 10/21/12 8:59 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:

...
> model {
>    real intercept;
>    real slope;
>    real mu[N];
>
>    for (i in 1:N) {
>      intercept <- beta + u2_z[school[i]] * sigma_u2 ;
>      slope <- gamma + v2_z[year[i]] * sigma_v2 ;

>      mu[i] <- intercept + slope ;
>    }

...

Ben's right.  This should parse.  And it does if
the variable "intercept" is renamed to something
that doesn't start with "int".  This will be a problem
for any variable whose name has a prefix that matches
a ype (like "real").

The problem is that the "int" in "intercept" is
getting parsed as the beginning of a declaration
of variable "ercept"!  I need to only match "int"
as starting a declaration if the next char is not
alphanumeric or "_".

I'll commit a patch for the 1.0.3 release next week.

On 10/21/12 7:02 AM, Daniel Lee wrote:> On Oct 21, 2012, at 6:31 AM, Joe King <joeki...@yahoo.com

<mailto:joeki...@yahoo.com>> wrote:
 >
 >> Thanks for your reply, though I am a bit confused. There are no predictors in this model (yet).
 >
 > I think Bob meant to type "year[i]" instead of "school[i]" or "x[i]" in his last post.

I may have the terminology wrong here, but I thought
a "slope" was something you multiplied by a predictor.
The model Daniel suggested (see above) looks to me
like a multilevel model with two varying intercepts.

- Bob

structures.

Stan just has a base reader class from which a model
reads data.

In the command-line code, it's implemented
with a dump reader (which doesn't yet handle all the
creative variation in R's dump() output).

In RStan, it's implemented in RStan to read from
an R object.  So that'd be the place to look for
what's going on with the types.

I'm guessing the following intended behavior may have
something to do with it:

The model will issue calls to read integer arrays
(for integer arrays in a Stan model) or double arrays
(for everything else).  If the input is integers, it
should still be readable as a double by casting.

That's what the dump() reader implementation does and
is what the RStan implementation should do.

- Bob

up to a proportion.  For instance, you can use something like:

It's a red herring as far as modeling goes.  Any choice

Half Cauchy is the easiest in Stan, because you don't even
need the half part because we only need to compute the probability

messages.body_plain:
On 10/22/12 3:57 PM, Joe King wrote:> Thanks again Bob

 >
 > Can you tell me how I provide initial values in RStan ? I looked in the manual but didn't see anything except in 4.2
 > about command line options...

The manual doesn't cover RStan arguments.  Use
help(rstan) and follow the index for a list of
functions and help(stan) for the arguments to stan().

There are multiple ways to do it, but the "standard"
way to do it is with a function.

Here's an example from a model I just ran:

Model params (Stan)

...
parameters {
   simplex[K] pi;               // prevalence of categories
   simplex[K] theta[J,K];       // response of anotator j to category k
}
...

R inits (R)

piVote <- rep(0,K);
...
thetaVote <- array(NA,c(J,K,K));
...

Define the function (R):

init_fun = function() {
   return(list(pi=piVote,
               theta=thetaVote));
}

Call the fit function (R):

fit <- stan(file="dawid-skene.stan",
            init=init_fun,
            data=data_list,
            iter=500, chains=4);

- Bob

messages.subject: Traceplot in rstan
messages.body_plain:
Hi Team Stan,

I was using the traceplot function in rstan and had a thought. If I use just

traceplot(stanfit)

I get traceplots of all the parameters stacked one above another. If there are many parameters, which is likely the case for many complex models for which stan is especially useful, this is difficult to visualize as everything gets compressed (unless on a very large monitor). In RStudio, which is becoming hugely popular, these plots often can't be printed at all because they are bigger than the plot window (a limitation of RStudio that I hope gets fixed someday). I was wondering if other people thought that it would be more pleasing to have traceplot works like it does in coda and have the plots appear in succession each time the user hits enter?

One possible workaround currently would be to write a loop function for traceplot using the pars option.

Also, one very minor suggestion (if it's easy) would be to reset the traceplot layout panel after use. For example, right now if I run

traceplot(stanfit)

then decide to just look at one parameter in more detail and run

traceplot(stanfit, pars = 'beta')

it plots beta up in the top and leaves blank space for all the other plots. It's easy for me to reset it by running

par(mfrow = c(1,1)

after the first traceplot, but I just thought this was unnecessary if it could be automatically reset after running the traceplot function. Anyway, this is not a priority by any means and might not be preferable for all users. I just thought I'd make the suggestion since I noticed it.

Thanks again for all your work on this great package and program and also for all your help getting me started with it.
Dan

> Sorry to keep going on about it, but this is what I am trying to replicate (I highlighted them in red)
>
> > fit.lme4.all <- lmer(outcome ~1 + (year-1|school.ID),data=dt.all)
> > summary(fit.lme4.all)
> Linear mixed model fit by REML
> Formula: outcome ~ 1 + (year - 1 | school.ID)
>    Data: dt.all
>     AIC    BIC logLik deviance REMLdev
>  183343 183410 -91664   183325  183327
> Random effects:
>  Groups    Name     Variance  Std.Dev. Corr
>  school.ID year2004   0.94242  0.97078
>            year2005  20.03281  4.47580  0.016
>            year2006 324.96381 18.02675 -0.233 -0.137
>  Residual            25.26760  5.02669
> Number of obs: 30000, groups: school.ID, 100
>
> Fixed effects:
>             Estimate Std. Error t value
> (Intercept)  19.9286     0.1021   195.2

I have finally been able to replicate this result reasonably well. The fundamental problem was that the above lmer() model is fairly different from the original .stan code. This model has a single, fixed intercept and the coefficients on the 3 year variables vary by school (of which there are 100). I tend to think of a 100x3 matrix of coefficients whose rows are assumed to be multivariate normal with an unknown mean vector, an unknown diagonal matrix of standard deviations, and an unknown correlation matrix. So, in order to get something that resembles the above, we have to parameterize the .stan file accordingly. I'll attach the entire code but discuss it in blocks because it is a useful example.

The data are the same, except that I centered the outcome variable in R.
data {
    int<lower=1> n2 ;    // number of schools
    int<lower=1> N ;     // number of students
    int<lower=1> N_year; // number of years
    real y[N] ;          // outcome
    int school[N] ;      // school id
    int year[N] ;        // year {1,2 or 3}
}

The parameters are a bit different than what you originally specified. The year variable has three levels, and I'm treating the first as the baseline. Thus, I'm constraining the expectation of the first coefficient to be zero and letting the other two contrast with it.
parameters {
    real alpha;            // intercept
    vector[N_year-1] beta; // 2nd and 3rd expected slopes (first is constrained to be 0.0)
    real<lower=0> sigma ;  // standard error of regression
    matrix[n2,N_year] slopes_z; // z-score of the slopes
    corr_matrix[N_year] Tau; // correlation matrix of the slopes
    real<lower=0> tau[N_year]; // standard deviations of the slopes
}

I now use the "Multivariate Matt Trick" (also mentioned by Terrance) where quantities that have a multivariate normal distribution under the theoretical model are in practice, expressed as a function of standard normals and a Cholesky factor. See

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariate_normal_distribution#Drawing_values_from_the_distribution

model {
  real mu[N];
  int k;
  matrix[n2,N_year] slopes_error;
  slopes_error <- slopes_z * transpose(cholesky_decompose(Tau)) ;

  for (i in 1:N) {

    k <- year[i];
    mu[i] <- alpha + (if_else(k - 1, beta[k - 1], 0.0) +
                       tau[k] * slopes_error[school[i],k]);
  }

What I call slopes_error (almost) corresponds to transpose(Az) in the Wikipedia notation. The difference is that that Tau is a correlation matrix rather than a covariance matrix, so we have to scale by the standard deviations (tau). The last line says that if k > 1, add beta[k-1] plus tau[k] times the appropriate element of schools_error, and if k = 1, then just use 0.0 for the expected baseline. The rest of the model {} block is straightforward, just a likelihood and a bunch of weakly informative priors priors (except on Tau, which is implicitly jointly uniform):

  y ~ normal(mu,sigma);
  for (j in 1:N_year) {
     tau[j] ~ cauchy(0.0,5.0) ;
     col(slopes_z,j) ~ normal(0, 1) ;
  }
  alpha ~ cauchy(0.0,5.0);
  beta ~ cauchy(0.0,5.0);
  sigma ~ cauchy(0.0,5.0);
  // implicit: Tau ~ lkj_corr(1.0);
}

Even with all that, it is still a bit difficult to sample from this posterior efficiently. I get

messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, October 23, 2012 3:12:52 PM UTC-4, Joe King wrote:
> Do you mean I should centre the outcome in R first with something like
> outcome <- outcome - mean(outcome)

Yes, for a fully observed outcome (i.e. the sample mean can be estimated), that is often a good idea with Stan and is what I did. In principle, it shouldn't be necessary but in practice it makes the default initial values of the parameters more plausible. There is not much cost to it, as long as you remember that it shifts the estimated intercept of the model.

> Also, would it make much difference if I use a implicit uniform prior on the parameters instead of cauchy ? I know how to do that with <lower=, upper> in the parameter section but how do I do that for the vector ?

You can do it the same way, you just indicate the length of the vector at the end. In fact, I did so in the previous post

real<lower=0> tau[N_year]; // standard deviations of the slopes

An implicit uniform prior on the taus over some reasonable bounded interval would probably yield about the same results. An improper or barely proper prior probably wouldn't yield the same results.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
On 10/23/12 4:32 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> OK, now I have a question (forgive me if the answer's already in the manual).  Suppose I define a parameter theta to
> have a normal (mu, sigma) distribution but then theta is declared as real<lower=0, upper=0.5>.  Does Stan then work with
> the truncated normal density (i.e., getting the correct normalizing factor which is now a function of mu and sigma) or
> does it just use the normal density without adjusting for the truncation?

First, you never get the full normalization term in Stan.
All constant terms are dropped.  In the normal, we never
include the constant normalizing term -log(sqrt(2*pi)).

The difference between

    x ~ normal(mu,sigma);   // no space before '('!!!

and

    x ~ normal(mu,sigma) T[0,0.5];

is that the latter applies the truncated density and
the former does not.

If the variable x is declared as real<lower=0,upper=0.5>,
that is, with fixed bounds, then the first is OK as
we only need the density up to a proportion.  If the
bounds were variable, you'd need the second form.

Assuming the bounds are properly declared for x,
we should be able to implicitly drop the truncation
in the future, but the code doesn't do that yet (it also
doesn't check ranges for x and return -inf if x is not
in the specified bounds and it probably should).

- Bob

Hmm, now I'm confused.  Here's what I think you're saying.  Consider 3 possibilities:

1.
real theta
theta ~ normal (mu,sigma)

2.
real<lower=0,upper=0.5> theta
theta ~ normal (mu, sigma)

3.
real<lower=0,upper=0.5> theta
theta ~ normal (mu, sigma) T[0,0.5]

4.
real theta
theta ~ normal (mu, sigma) T[0,0.5]

As I understand it, option 1 does the log of the normal density (ignoring the -log(sqrt(2*pi)), which I'll ignore in the rest of this discussion).
Option 2 also uses the log of the normal density, but theta is constrained.  So it's not doing the truncated normal distribution, it's doing something else (I suppose it's equivalent to the truncated distribution with a weird prior on (mu,sigma)).
Option 3 is doing the log of the truncated normal density (i.e., including the normalizing factor that depends on (mu,sigma)).
Option 4 . . . I don't know what that's doing.  Perhaps it is also doing the truncated density, just with an inefficient implementation in that theta is not being subjected to a transformation for computational purposes?

messages.subject: Stan 1.0.3 Released
messages.body_plain:
The Stan Development Team is happy to announce the
availability of Stan and RStan versions 1.0.3.  See:

    http://mc-stan.org/

Stan now supports lower and upper bounds in vector and
matrix declarations and vectorization of all univariate
continuous probability functions.

RStan now supports running chains in multiple processes
and merging the results.

We've also fixed some bugs and hopefully made user error
messages more comprehensible.

The important issues dealt with in the release are as follows.

v 1.0.3 Release Notes (25 Oct 2012)
======================================================================
Stan Bug Fixes:
  -- error output in stanc now directed to standard error
  -- catching all exceptions thrown in stanc to prevent core dumps
  -- parser now accepts variable names starting with "int" and "real"
     in first assignment after declaration
  -- now catching unknown truncation cdfs and vectorizations in stanc
  -- (hopefully) less scary message for domain error rejects
  -- removed use of assert(); replaced with exceptions where
     appropriate
  -- fixed boundary condition on reporting max init retry failures
  -- fixed initialization errors in tests that failed on some platforms
  -- improved error checking for matrix size args to prevent segfaults
  -- fixed boundary condition on bounded transform to allow
     beta(0.8,0.8) samples near 0 or 1
Stan New Features:
  -- mdivide_left_tri_low, mdivide_right_tri_low functions
  -- all univariate continuous densities vectorized
  -- better error checking for transforms
  -- new error return type in stanc for invalid arguments
  -- lower and upper bounds for vectors, row vectors, and matrices
  -- command parameter refresh <= 0 turns off iteration reporting
  -- int divisions produce warnings in stanc
  -- errors caused by invalid transformed parameters include var name
  -- various efficiency improvements and error handling for boundary
     conditions and special cases of probability functions
  -- simplified matrix code with heavier use of templating
Stan Manual Additions:
  -- example of defining new distribution with parameters
  -- diff report vs. previous versions
  -- updated for range constraints on vector, row vector, matrix
  -- updated Eigen licensing information (now MPL, was LGPL)
  -- fixed alpha ordering issue in function index due to bolding
RStan Bug Fixes:
  -- bug of setting parameter epsilon_pm wrongly for NUTS
  -- fixed seed reset so results match Stan
RStan New Features:
  -- return empty stanfit object upon error such as incorrect data
     input, wrong argument specification, etc. Previously, it will
     stop. The empty stanfit includes the compiled model, so it can be
     reused.
  -- add function stan_demo() to run examples included in Stan.
  -- add function sflist2stanfit() to merge a list of stanfit objects
     into one, to facilitate user-level parallelism.
  -- add S3 method as.matrix, as.array, is.array, dim,
     dimnames for stanfit objects.
  -- specify seed using string of digits in addition to numbers
  -- turn off refresh if value <= 0
======================================================================

As usual, let us know on the users list or on our issue tracker
if there are problems.

- Stan Development Team

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Fitting an ODE model with stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Fitting an ODE model with stan
messages.body_plain:
This would likely have to be implemented directly in C++
(http://mc-stan.org/cpp-quickstart.html) as a new model by coding up
the gradients explicitly (derivatives with respect to the parameters
would just give new ODEs on which you should be able to use the same
integrator).  This way Stan can proceed with HMC without dealing with
the autodiff problems.

On Fri, Oct 26, 2012 at 1:05 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> On Friday, October 26, 2012 10:52:50 AM UTC-4, José Rojas Echenique wrote:
>>
>> I'm working with an ODE model of cellular metabolism (~10 reactions and
>> ~50 parameters some of which are known pretty accurately some not at all).
>> I have C code to time integrate the equations for a given set of parameters.
>> I want to fit a model where the likelihood is normal centered at the ODE
>> solution.
>
>
> I am guessing this would be difficult. One of the things that makes Stan's
> implementation of HMC great is that it uses auto-differentiation to
> calculate the gradient of the log posterior with respect to the parameters.
> However, if your problem requires sending the parameters to an external
> subroutine, then somehow you have got to slip the derivatives back into the
> right places when the baton is passed back to Stan.
>
> In general, you might have a model something like this
>
> data {
>   ...
> }
> parameters {
>   ...
> }
> transformed parameters {
>   real mu[K];
>   mu <- SomeFunctionOfParameters();
> }
> model {
>   // optional priors
>   outcome ~ normal(mu,sigma);
> }
>
> The above works fine in Stan iff SomeFunctionOfParameters() is explicit (and
> utilizes functions that are available in Stan). We have talked about adding
> support for solving for the root of an arbitrary implicit function and
> teaching Stan implicit differentiation, but there isn't a firm plan on that
> yet.
>
> There was someone else who was interested in ODEs and Stan. Bob would
> remember the name. If you really, really wanted to implement the
> infrastructure to make it work in Stan, it would probably be good to
> coordinate efforts because it would be a big undertaking.
>
> Ben
>

> --
>
>

messages.body_plain: I'm having a problem compiling Stan 1.0.3 after modifying a source file (~/stan-src-1.0.3/src/stan/gm/command.hpp). After invoking make bin/libstan.a and make bin/stanc, make replies that the targets are up to date, which is unexpected. Shouldn't make see that there is a file which has changed and then recompile that file? What am I doing wrong? Of course, I can run make clean-all, and then recompile everything, but that is too slow. Thanks in advance for any ideas you may have.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] compiling stan after changing a source file
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] compiling stan after changing a source file
messages.body_plain:
The makefile behavior in this case is correct. The generated model
needs to be recompiled when gm/command.hpp changes, not bin/stanc.
That means, if you have model.stan, model.cpp is going to be the same
before and after changes to gm/command.hpp.

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan 1.0.3 Released
messages.body_plain:
Hello stan developers,  I attach an Rstan script and some sample data.   You've already generously provided me with feedback on model constructions over more complex versions.   So I send this note to suggest that this model should not fail under Rstan 1.0.3, but it does; actually, it crashes the R session.   I'm not asking for debugging help, but thought it may be useful for you to have an example of a model that absolutely will not run in stan (where variations of it do under BUGS solvers).   The model augments the data likelihood over multiple statements under differing data types.   The multiple data blocks express a dependence through sharing a common set of multivariate nested random effects.   Each random effect term is multivariate on a set of latent indices so that the 'rows' are each sampled in a multivariate fashion.   I've employed one of the stan developer tricks to avoid repeated inversion and gradient computation and storing over multiple NUTS steps for the covariance matrices over repeated sampling draws of the multivariate random effects.   Anyway, my guess is that the repeated sampling of a multivariate latent object is the problem.   While I've seen implementations of stan models on the list that perform a single multivariate parameters draw, I've not seen any that perform multiple such draws.   But i don't know.   At this point, I'm quite sure the issue isn't the model concept or the data and I suspect the model triggers a stan bug.  It bears brief mention that the same problem persists, no matter the prior formulations and their degree of informativeness.

Terrance.

>  -- specify seed using string of digits in addition to numbers
>  -- turn off refresh if value <= 0

>
> As usual, let us know on the users list or on our issue tracker

>
> - Stan Development Team

Hi Terrance,

If you follow the procedure for a runtime error at

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/4gv3fNCqSNk/FXHj6fn0SC0J

then (even without gdb) the (or at least, a) problem is apparent:

goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/tmp/SU/tds$ ./ordMultiProt_E_test --data=datstan_mp.Rdump

Exception: INDEX OPERATOR [] OUT OF BOUNDS; index=1215; lower bound=1; upper bound=1214; index position=1; c3

Diagnostic information:
Dynamic exception type: std::out_of_range
std::exception::what: INDEX OPERATOR [] OUT OF BOUNDS; index=1215; lower bound=1; upper bound=1214; index position=1; c3

So, one of your loops goes to c3[1215] when it only has 1214 rows. A quick grep reveals

goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/tmp/SU/tds$ grep -n c3 ordMultiProt_E_test.stan
101:    matrix[N2,D3] c3;
128:            for( i in 1:N3 ) for( d in 1:D3 ) c3[i,d]       <- Delta[teacher3[i],(D1+D2+d)] + Phi[section3[i],(D1+D2+d)] + Theta[session3[i],(D1+D2+d)] + Beta[rater3[i],(D1+D2+d)];
159:    for(i in 1:N3) for(d in 1:D3) y3[i,d]   ~ ordered_logistic(c3[i,d],gamma3[d]);

So, you are looping to N3 but c3 has only N2 rows.

Ben

Ben wrote this:

>     goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/tmp/SU/tds$ ./ordMultiProt_E_test --data=datstan_mp.Rdump

>     Dynamic exception type: std::out_of_range
>     std::exception::what: INDEX OPERATOR [] OUT OF BOUNDS; index=1215; lower bound=1; upper bound=1214; index position=1; c3

1.  I should've paid more attention to Ben's output.
It's good that Stan's picking up the error -- this is
what it's supposed to do.

Is the exception causing RStan to crash?  If so, we
probably just need to put a catch in the appropriate place
to write the exception's type and message back to the R stderr
stream.

I'm not sure what happens during I/O.  Our message could
be a lot better in terms of identifying what was going on
when the error occurred (I/O or model, specifically).

As is, I only know from looking at the code that it arose
when some function called stan::math::raise_range_error,
which throws a std::out_of_range exception.

2.  I'd like to figure out a simpler policy for RStan user
error reporting than having them run through Stan command
line.  It just seems like too much of an installation and
manual reading exercise for an error report.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I did not try this example.  But tried a simple one:

parameters {
    real y[1];
}

model {
    y[2] ~ normal(0, 1);
}

In RStan, if we set_cppo('debug'), R would not crash for this example.  set_cppo('debug') would not set -DNDEBUG flag. By default, Stan does not set this flag.  If -DNDEBUG is set in Stan, Stan will exit with a segfault for this example.

When set_cppo('debug') is set in RStan, for this example, R would not crash.

> set_cppo('debug')
mode debug for compiling C++ code is set
>
> scode <- '
+ parameters {
+  real y[1];
+ }
+

+ model {
+  y[2] ~ normal(0, 1);
+ }
+ '

>
> library(rstan)
> a <- stan(model_code = scode, iter = 10, chains = 1)
TRANSLATING MODEL 'scode' FROM Stan CODE TO C++ CODE NOW.

messages.subject: defining a covariance matrix from a correlation matrix
messages.subject_clean: defining a covariance matrix from a correlation matrix
messages.body_plain:
Hi,  I finally got one of my monster multivariate models lofted in stan.  (see attached script).   I constructed a set of covariance matrices from an associated set of correlation matrices, the latter under uniform priors.   The manner in which I was able to get this to run was to declare the covariance matrices as unstructured matrix objects, rather than cov_matrix objects.  I had been receiving error messages under the cov_matrix declaration of the first-used matrix that the sampler failed for violation of symmetry.   That said, the error occurred so rapidly that I wonder if there it never got to the sampler.   These covariance matrices are, in turn, used to generate multivariate gaussian samples.   The cholesky decomposition of each covariance matrix is rendered for that purpose.   So the chains may yet crash under an SPD error, but I wanted to let you know of this event.

Lastly, I think previous run attempts crashed R because I input a NULL data element.

--
Thank you, Terrance Savitsky

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Fitting an ODE model with stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Fitting an ODE model with stan
messages.body_plain:
An alternative might be to build a templated implementation of the ODE
solver in c++ that replaces every instance of the typename double with
a template parameter T. Then Stan could do autodiff on the solver.
(That's right, isn't it?)

However, the cost in both time and memory could well be prohibitive.
Implementing the derivatives by hand would certainly be much faster,
if it's feasible.

Matt

On Fri, Oct 26, 2012 at 11:20 AM, Michael Betancourt
<betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> This would likely have to be implemented directly in C++
> (http://mc-stan.org/cpp-quickstart.html) as a new model by coding up
> the gradients explicitly (derivatives with respect to the parameters
> would just give new ODEs on which you should be able to use the same
> integrator).  This way Stan can proceed with HMC without dealing with
> the autodiff problems.
>
> On Fri, Oct 26, 2012 at 1:05 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> On Friday, October 26, 2012 10:52:50 AM UTC-4, José Rojas Echenique wrote:
>>>
>>> I'm working with an ODE model of cellular metabolism (~10 reactions and
>>> ~50 parameters some of which are known pretty accurately some not at all).
>>> I have C code to time integrate the equations for a given set of parameters.
>>> I want to fit a model where the likelihood is normal centered at the ODE
>>> solution.
>>
>>
>> I am guessing this would be difficult. One of the things that makes Stan's
>> implementation of HMC great is that it uses auto-differentiation to
>> calculate the gradient of the log posterior with respect to the parameters.
>> However, if your problem requires sending the parameters to an external
>> subroutine, then somehow you have got to slip the derivatives back into the
>> right places when the baton is passed back to Stan.
>>
>> In general, you might have a model something like this
>>
>> data {
>>   ...
>> }
>> parameters {
>>   ...
>> }
>> transformed parameters {
>>   real mu[K];
>>   mu <- SomeFunctionOfParameters();
>> }
>> model {
>>   // optional priors
>>   outcome ~ normal(mu,sigma);
>> }
>>
>> The above works fine in Stan iff SomeFunctionOfParameters() is explicit (and
>> utilizes functions that are available in Stan). We have talked about adding
>> support for solving for the root of an arbitrary implicit function and
>> teaching Stan implicit differentiation, but there isn't a firm plan on that
>> yet.
>>
>> There was someone else who was interested in ODEs and Stan. Bob would
>> remember the name. If you really, really wanted to implement the
>> infrastructure to make it work in Stan, it would probably be good to
>> coordinate efforts because it would be a big undertaking.
>>
>> Ben
>>
>> --
>>
>>
>

> --
>
>

messages.body_plain:
It would be nice.  Does R let you specify ragged
arrays some way?

There's always the explicit DB-like coding of a ragged
array using the indices.  Suppose x is a ragged array
of size I, where the entry for index i in 1:I is
an array of size N[i].

   K |  ii  nn  word
   ------------------
   1 |   1   1    17
   2 |   1   2   192
   3 |   1   3    42
      ...
   92|   1   92  598
   93|   2   1    17
   94|   2   2     3
   95|   2   3   971

The matrix x is determined by:

   x[ ii[k], nn[k] ]  =  word[k]

If we assume the ii and nn are sorted as above, we can
use an index structure to indicate where the entries
for x[i,] start:

   I|   kk
   -------
   1|    1
   2|   93
   ...

So kk[i] is the entry where the entries for x[i,] start
and size(x[i,]) in the ragged array is (kk[i+1] - kk[i])
(assuming you pad one on the end).

With this secondary kk structure, you can do away with the
i and n indices and just keep the word array.

For a start, it'd be easy to write a Stan operation

   ragged_array_of_arrays(word,k)

that would take those word and start arrays and create a
ragged array of arrays.  The same kind of thing would work
for a vector.

But there's no good type for the result in Stan.  We
could always add something like:

   int  x[I,];

for a ragged array of arrays of ints.

I also could imagine specifying a ragged array in Stan
by providing its indexes.

   int<lower=0> N;            // size of ragged array
   int<lower=0> x_sizes[N];   // size of each entry of ragged array
   ragged_array x[x_sizes];   // ragged array

That's more than a bit clunky, but it would be
workable given what we have now.

Essentially x_sizes[N] is just the diff of kk with itself
offset by one.

- Bob

On Mon, Oct 29, 2012 at 2:46 PM, Matt Hoffman <mdho...@cs.princeton.edu> wrote:

> An alternative might be to build a templated implementation of the ODE
> solver in c++ that replaces every instance of the typename double with
> a template parameter T. Then Stan could do autodiff on the solver.
> (That's right, isn't it?)

Yeah, that's right although the gradients may not be great depending on the solver.  Simple solvers (like Euler integration) could be done directly in the Stan modelling language without too much trouble and would work just fine.  More complex ones (like adaptive stepsize methods, implicit integrators, etc) would have some discontinuities which could hurt.  That said, I'd expect them to work OK.

>
> However, the cost in both time and memory could well be prohibitive.
> Implementing the derivatives by hand would certainly be much faster,
> if it's feasible.

The cost, particularly for implicit methods, would be quite expensive and could be avoided with clever hand-calculated derivatives.

All of this said, ODE fitting can often be reformulated in terms of fitting temporal derivatives of your data in which case you're not at all required to differentiate through the ODE solver.  E.G., if you have dy = f(y,theta) and you want to fit theta given some ys then you can compute the dy's given the ys using finite differences (or, if you want to get fancy, represent them as latent variables...)  and you no longer need to do the forward simulation.

Cheers,
Marcus

On Tue, Oct 30, 2012 at 4:59 PM, José Rojas Echenique
<jose.i...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> All of this said, ODE fitting can often be reformulated in terms of fitting
>> temporal derivatives of your data in which case you're not at all required
>> to differentiate through the ODE solver.
>
>> E.G., if you have dy = f(y,theta)
>> and you want to fit theta given some ys then you can compute the dy's given
>> the ys using finite differences (or, if you want to get fancy, represent
>> them as latent variables...)  and you no longer need to do the forward
>> simulation.
>
> I'm not sure I understand what you mean here.  Finite differences?
> Using rates of change of the data as the dy's?

If you have a time series y_0, ..., y_T that you want to fit an ODE dy
= f(y,theta) then one thing you can do is write (using a backwards
difference):

dy_i = (y_{i} - y_{i-1}) / dt

and try to fit the model

dy_i ~ normal(f(y,theta),sigma)

This has a number of drawbacks but avoids many of the issues of
fitting ODEs.  If your time step (dt) is sufficiently small for the
phenomena you want to model, then this will tend to work ok.
(Alternatively, if your dt is large and your ODE solver requires many
small steps or high order methods to advance dt, then it's not likely
to work as well.)

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Kriging Model
messages.body_plain:
You're mixing scalars and vectors and arrays.  For instance,

  for( n in 1:N )
    W[n] ~ multi_normal(muW[n], Omega[n]);

Omega is a single covariance matrix so Omega[n] is referring to a
single column of omega and muW is an array of N scalars so muW[n] is
just a single scalar.  Same with W[n] and X[n] in the dot product
line.  Perhaps you just want:

W ~ multi_normal(muW,Omega);

Also beyond those issues, your line:

  for( n in 1:N )
    mu[n] ~ dot_product(X[n],beta) + W[n];

doesn't make sense.  ~ must always have a distribution on the right
hand side, not a statement.  If you're trying to assign something to
mu[n] then you need to use <- and, in this case, you can't because mu
is a parameter.  If you want it saved, then you should make mu a
transformed parameter.  Otherwise, you should just make it a local
variable.

Hopefully this helps!

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Kriging Model
messages.body_plain:
It looks like beta should be in the parameters, not transformed
parameters, block as it's never set in there.

Also, why are you only ever using the first column of X and the first
entry of beta?  Perhaps you mean:

mu <- X * beta + W

where you change the types to be:

vector[N] mu;
vector[p] beta;

You never actually use those other entries otherwise.

Regarding the negative scale parameters, you need to constrain
errorprec and spatprec to be positive.  E.G.,

real<lower=0> errorprec;

Also, your last line is using the precision parameter, but the normal
distribution takes a standard deviation parameter.  That line could
also be made much faster.  E.G., just write

Y ~ normal(mu,sqrt(errsq));

instead of the for loop.  This takes advantage of vectorization
internally.  Not a huge point, but it will be a big difference in
speed for large N.

Cheers,
Marcus

On Wednesday, October 31, 2012 1:28:44 PM UTC-4, Marcus wrote:
> Also, your last line is using the precision parameter, but the normal
> distribution takes a standard deviation parameter.

Also, the multivariate normal distribution in BUGS is parameterized in terms of the precision matrix, whereas in Stan it is parameterized in terms of the covariance matrix. So, instead of

W ~ multi_normal(muW, Omega);

you should do

W ~ multi_normal(muW, H);

and not even define Omega.

Ben
